questions.stem: Which term describes the nutrients the body needs in large amounts and that supply energy measured in calories?

rationales.whyCorrect: Macronutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, and fats (with water sometimes included), required in gram-level amounts each day, and the three energy-yielding classes provide the calories the body uses for fuel. Micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) are needed in much smaller milligram or microgram amounts and do not themselves supply energy. Distinguishing these categories is the foundation for understanding energy balance and diet planning.
rationales.eli10: Think of your body like a car. Macronutrients are the big tank of gasoline you pour in by the gallon to make the engine go, while micronutrients are the tiny drops of oil that keep the parts working. 'Macro' means big, so macronutrients are the big, energy-giving foods: carbs, proteins, and fats.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly identifies an essential nutrient?

options.text: A nutrient the body can make in sufficient amounts from other compounds
A nutrient that provides the largest number of calories per gram of food
A nutrient that is found only in animal-based foods and never in plants
A nutrient the body cannot make in adequate amounts, so it must come from food

rationales.whyCorrect: An essential nutrient is one the body cannot synthesize at all or cannot make in amounts sufficient to meet its needs, so it must be obtained from the diet; examples include certain amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals. This is unrelated to caloric density or food source. The concept explains why dietary variety matters for preventing deficiency diseases.
rationales.eli10: Some things your body is like a little factory for and can build on its own. But a few important parts it just cannot manufacture, so you HAVE to eat them, kind of like a recipe that calls for an ingredient you can only get from the store. Those must-eat ingredients are the 'essential' nutrients.

This is unrelated to caloric density or food source. The concept explains why dietary variety matters for preventing deficiency diseases.

questions.stem: Which macronutrient provides the greatest amount of energy per gram?

rationales.whyCorrect: Fat supplies about 9 kilocalories per gram, more than double the roughly 4 kilocalories per gram from carbohydrate and protein. This high energy density is why fats are an efficient long-term energy store in the body. Fiber, a type of carbohydrate that is largely indigestible, contributes little usable energy.
rationales.eli10: Imagine packing a suitcase. Fat is like a super-compressed bag that stuffs the most energy into the smallest space, giving 9 calories in each gram, while carbs and protein only pack about 4. That is why your body loves to store extra energy as fat: it fits a lot into a little.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of dietary protein in the body?

options.text: To supply amino acids for building and repairing body tissues
To serve as the body's first and preferred source of quick energy
To transport fat-soluble vitamins through the bloodstream
To provide long-term insulation and cushioning of organs

rationales.whyCorrect: Protein's chief role is structural and functional: it provides amino acids used to build and repair muscle, enzymes, hormones, and other tissues. Although protein can be used for energy, carbohydrate is the body's preferred quick fuel, and fat handles insulation and vitamin transport. Understanding protein's building role clarifies why intake needs rise during growth, healing, and illness.
rationales.eli10: Protein is like a box of LEGO bricks. Your body pulls the bricks (amino acids) out of the box and snaps them together to build muscles and fix parts that get worn out. You can burn the bricks for heat in an emergency, but that would be a waste; their real job is building.

Although protein can be used for energy, carbohydrate is the body's preferred quick fuel, and fat handles insulation and vitamin transport. questions.stem: Which comparison between fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins is accurate?

options.text: Water-soluble vitamins are stored extensively in body fat, while fat-soluble vitamins are not stored
Fat-soluble vitamins can be stored in the body and are more likely to reach toxic levels from excess intake
Water-soluble vitamins require dietary fat for absorption, while fat-soluble vitamins do not
Fat-soluble vitamins are excreted rapidly in urine, while water-soluble vitamins are retained

rationales.whyCorrect: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) are stored in the liver and fatty tissues, so consistently high intakes can accumulate and cause toxicity. Water-soluble vitamins (B-complex and C) are generally not stored to a large degree and excess is excreted in the urine, making toxicity less likely but daily intake more important. This distinction guides safe supplement use.
rationales.eli10: Fat-soluble vitamins are like guests who move into your house and stay, so if too many show up it gets crowded and causes trouble (toxicity). Water-soluble vitamins are like guests who leave the same day, washing out in your pee, so you need to keep inviting new ones but they rarely overcrowd.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) are stored in the liver and fatty tissues, so consistently high intakes can accumulate and cause toxicity. Water-soluble vitamins (B-complex and C) are generally not stored to a large degree and excess is excreted in the urine, making toxicity less likely but daily intake more important. This distinction guides safe supplement use.

questions.stem: Which change would most likely cause a person to be in positive energy balance over time?

options.text: Consuming fewer calories than the body expends each day
Consuming calories roughly equal to daily energy expenditure
Consuming more calories than the body expends each day
Increasing physical activity without changing food intake

rationales.whyCorrect: Positive energy balance occurs when energy intake exceeds energy expenditure, and the surplus is stored, typically as body fat, leading to weight gain over time. Eating less than expenditure produces negative balance and weight loss, while matching the two maintains weight. This framework underlies weight management guidance.
rationales.eli10: Picture a bank account for energy. If you put in more money (calories eaten) than you spend (calories burned), the balance grows and gets stored as fat. 'Positive' just means the account is filling up because more is coming in than going out.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Positive energy balance occurs when energy intake exceeds energy expenditure, and the surplus is stored, typically as body fat, leading to weight gain over time. Eating less than expenditure produces negative balance and weight loss, while matching the two maintains weight. This framework underlies weight management guidance.

questions.stem: Why is water often classified as an essential nutrient even though it provides no calories?

options.text: Because the body stores large water reserves inside fat tissue and burns them for energy while fasting
Because digestion converts water into carbohydrate, giving cells a backup supply of usable glucose
Because it transports substances, drives reactions, and cools the body, yet is lost faster than made
Because it directly supplies most of the vitamins and minerals the body requires over a full day

rationales.whyCorrect: Water is essential because the body loses it continuously through urine, sweat, and breathing and produces far less metabolic water than it loses, so intake must replace those losses daily. It serves as the medium for metabolic reactions, transports nutrients and wastes, and helps regulate body temperature. It qualifies as a nutrient despite contributing zero calories. Water is not stored in fat as an energy reserve (A), is never converted into carbohydrate (B), and is not itself the main source of vitamins and minerals (D).
rationales.eli10: Water does not give you energy like food, but it is the river everything floats on inside your body: it carries stuff around, helps chemical reactions happen, and cools you down when you sweat. Your body makes only a tiny bit of its own water and you lose it all day, so you must keep refilling, which is why it is 'essential.'
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Water is essential because the body loses it continuously through urine, sweat, and breathing and produces far less metabolic water than it loses, so intake must replace those losses daily. It serves as the medium for metabolic reactions, transports nutrients and wastes, and helps regulate body temperature. It qualifies as a nutrient despite contributing zero calories. Water is not stored in fat as an energy reserve (A), is never converted into carbohydrate (B), and is not itself the main source of vitamins and minerals (D).

questions.stem: A student eats a meal of white rice, a chicken breast, and olive oil-dressed vegetables. Which example correctly matches a food to the macronutrient it primarily contributes?

options.text: White rice is the meal's main source of complete protein
The olive oil is the meal's main source of fat
The chicken breast is the meal's main source of fiber
The vegetables are the meal's main source of dietary fat

rationales.whyCorrect: Olive oil is nearly pure fat, so it is the meal's leading fat contributor. White rice mainly supplies carbohydrate rather than complete protein, chicken breast is a protein source with little fiber, and vegetables provide fiber, vitamins, and minerals but little fat. Matching foods to their dominant macronutrient is a core skill in diet analysis.
rationales.eli10: Each food on the plate has a main job. Oil is basically liquid fat, so its job is fat. Rice brings the carbs, chicken brings the protein, and veggies bring the fiber and vitamins. The trick is spotting which food is the 'star player' for each nutrient.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Olive oil is nearly pure fat, so it is the meal's leading fat contributor. White rice mainly supplies carbohydrate rather than complete protein, chicken breast is a protein source with little fiber, and vegetables provide fiber, vitamins, and minerals but little fat. questions.stem: A person's diet consistently lacks a particular vitamin over many weeks. Which outcome would most likely result?

options.text: A deficiency disease as body stores and functions are depleted
Immediate toxicity symptoms from nutrient overload
An increase in the body's ability to synthesize that vitamin
Other vitamins in the diet would substitute for the missing one, preventing any problem

rationales.whyCorrect: When intake of a needed vitamin falls short over time, the body's reserves are used up and the biochemical processes that depend on it begin to fail, producing a deficiency disease (for example, scurvy from lack of vitamin C). The body cannot ramp up synthesis of an essential vitamin to compensate, and one vitamin generally cannot substitute for the specific function of another, so inadequate intake causes deficiency rather than toxicity. Recognizing this cause-and-effect explains classic deficiency conditions.
rationales.eli10: Vitamins are like batteries your body keeps in a drawer. If you stop restocking, the drawer slowly empties until the gadgets that need those batteries stop working, and that breakdown is a deficiency disease. A different vitamin cannot fill in, because each one runs its own specific gadgets.

questions.stem: A food label lists a serving that provides 20 grams of carbohydrate, 5 grams of protein, and 10 grams of fat. Which interpretation about the serving's energy is accurate?

options.text: Protein contributes the most calories because protein is the most concentrated fuel
Fat contributes more calories than the protein in this serving
Carbohydrate and fat contribute exactly the same number of calories
Carbohydrate contributes the most calories because it has the most grams

rationales.whyCorrect: Using the general values of 4 kcal per gram for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal per gram for fat, the fat provides about 90 kcal while the protein provides about 20 kcal, so fat clearly contributes more than protein. Carbohydrate at 20 grams gives about 80 kcal, which is less than the fat's 90 kcal and not equal to it, so having the most grams does not make carbohydrate the top calorie source. Applying energy-per-gram values lets you interpret how each nutrient adds to total calories.
rationales.eli10: Each gram of fat carries 9 calories, but each gram of carb or protein carries only 4. So even though there are more grams of carbs here, the fat still packs a bigger punch, and 10 grams of fat easily beats 5 grams of protein. It is like comparing heavy coins to light ones: fewer heavy coins can add up to more.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Using the general values of 4 kcal per gram for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal per gram for fat, the fat provides about 90 kcal while the protein provides about 20 kcal, so fat clearly contributes more than protein. Carbohydrate at 20 grams gives about 80 kcal, which is less than the fat's 90 kcal and not equal to it, so having the most grams does not make carbohydrate the top calorie source. questions.stem: What would most likely happen to a person's use of body protein if their diet provided very little carbohydrate and fat but adequate protein over several days?

options.text: The body would break down more protein for energy because its other fuels are lacking
Protein would be completely spared and reserved only for building and repairing tissue
The surplus protein would all be stored as new muscle despite the low energy intake
The body would stop using protein entirely in order to conserve it during the shortage

rationales.whyCorrect: When carbohydrate and fat, the body's usual energy fuels, are inadequate, the body turns to amino acids from dietary and body protein for energy, diverting protein away from its building and repair roles. Adequate carbohydrate and fat intake normally 'spares' protein for these functions, and the body cannot simply store extra protein as muscle without sufficient energy. This integration explains why balanced energy intake protects lean tissue.
rationales.eli10: Protein is your building crew, but if the furnace runs out of firewood (carbs and fat), the body starts burning the crew's LEGO bricks just to stay warm. When you eat enough carbs and fat, the crew gets to keep building instead of being thrown in the fire. That rescue is called 'protein sparing.'
rationales.distractorAnalysis: When carbohydrate and fat, the body's usual energy fuels, are inadequate, the body turns to amino acids from dietary and body protein for energy, diverting protein away from its building and repair roles. Adequate carbohydrate and fat intake normally 'spares' protein for these functions, and the body cannot simply store extra protein as muscle without sufficient energy. This integration explains why balanced energy intake protects lean tissue.

questions.stem: A snack bar high in added sugars supplies the same number of calories as a serving of plain yogurt with fruit. What does this illustrate about nutrient density?

options.text: The snack bar provides more vitamins and minerals per calorie than the yogurt
Both foods must provide identical amounts of micronutrients because their calories are equal
Nutrient density depends only on total calories, not on vitamin and mineral content
The yogurt provides more vitamins and minerals for the same number of calories

rationales.whyCorrect: Nutrient density describes the amount of beneficial nutrients such as vitamins and minerals a food provides relative to its calories, so plain yogurt with fruit (a source of calcium, protein, potassium, and B vitamins) delivers far more of these per calorie than a snack bar whose calories come largely from added sugars, often called empty calories. Equal calories therefore do not mean equal nutrition, and nutrient density is defined by nutrients per calorie rather than by calories alone. The Dietary Guidelines emphasize choosing nutrient-dense options to meet needs within calorie limits.
rationales.eli10: Imagine two backpacks that weigh exactly the same. The yogurt-and-fruit backpack is packed with useful gear (vitamins and minerals), while the sugary snack bar is stuffed mostly with foam that adds weight (calories) but does nothing helpful. Getting more useful gear for the same weight is what 'nutrient-dense' means.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Nutrient density describes the amount of beneficial nutrients such as vitamins and minerals a food provides relative to its calories, so plain yogurt with fruit (a source of calcium, protein, potassium, and B vitamins) delivers far more of these per calorie than a snack bar whose calories come largely from added sugars, often called empty calories. Equal calories therefore do not mean equal nutrition, and nutrient density is defined by nutrients per calorie rather than by calories alone. The Dietary Guidelines emphasize choosing nutrient-dense options to meet needs within calorie limits.

They are the body's main and preferred source of energy
They function primarily as the body's chief fat-storage molecule
They act mainly to transport oxygen through the blood

questions.stem: Why is dietary fiber classified as a carbohydrate that provides little or no usable energy to humans?

options.text: Fiber is chemically a lipid rather than a carbohydrate
Fiber is absorbed but immediately excreted by the kidneys
Fiber contains no carbon and therefore cannot be burned for fuel
Humans lack the enzymes needed to digest its bonds

rationales.whyCorrect: Fiber is a polysaccharide, but its bonds (such as the beta-linkages in cellulose) cannot be broken by human digestive enzymes, so it passes largely undigested. Because it is not broken into absorbable monosaccharides, it yields little energy while still providing benefits like promoting bowel regularity. It is genuinely a carbohydrate and does contain carbon.
rationales.eli10: Fiber is a carbohydrate, but it is locked with a special kind of clasp that human stomachs do not have the right key (enzyme) to open. So instead of being unlocked and used for energy, it travels through and helps sweep your digestive system clean. It is a carb your body cannot cash in.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Fiber is a polysaccharide, but its bonds (such as the beta-linkages in cellulose) cannot be broken by human digestive enzymes, so it passes largely undigested. questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of storing glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles?

options.text: To permanently convert excess glucose into structural fiber
To create a long-term fat store that cannot be broken down
To transport glucose out of the body through the urine
To provide a readily available reserve of glucose for energy needs

rationales.whyCorrect: Glycogen is the storage form of glucose in animals, kept mainly in the liver and muscles. When blood glucose falls or energy demand rises, glycogen is broken back down into glucose for quick use. Liver glycogen helps maintain blood glucose, while muscle glycogen fuels muscle activity.
rationales.eli10: When you have more sugar (glucose) than you need right now, your body packs it into a storage bundle called glycogen, like putting extra snacks in a backpack. Later, when you run low on energy, you unzip the backpack and grab the sugar back out fast. It is your quick-access energy stash.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Glycogen is the storage form of glucose in animals, kept mainly in the liver and muscles. questions.stem: Which change in a meal would most likely cause a slower, more gradual rise in blood glucose?

options.text: Choosing a high-fiber whole grain instead of a refined, low-fiber grain
Removing all fiber and eating only simple sugars
Drinking the carbohydrate as a sweetened beverage instead of eating it whole
Replacing the whole grain with a sugary refined grain product

rationales.whyCorrect: Fiber slows the digestion and absorption of carbohydrate, blunting the speed at which glucose enters the bloodstream. A high-fiber whole grain therefore produces a slower, more gradual glucose rise than a refined grain or a sugary drink, which are absorbed quickly. This is why whole grains are emphasized in the Dietary Guidelines.
rationales.eli10: Fiber acts like a speed bump for sugar entering your blood. Whole grains still have their fiber speed bumps, so the sugar trickles in slowly. Refined grains and sweet drinks have the speed bumps removed, so the sugar rushes in all at once. Slow and steady is what fiber gives you.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if a person consumed far too little carbohydrate over time and the body needed to protect blood glucose?

options.text: It would convert fatty acids directly into glucose to spare the brain
It would convert dietary fiber directly into large amounts of glucose
It would stop using glucose entirely, since no tissue truly requires it
It would make glucose from amino acids and increase ketone production from fat

rationales.whyCorrect: When carbohydrate is severely limited, the body makes glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as amino acids (gluconeogenesis) to protect essential glucose-dependent tissues, and it increases fat breakdown, producing ketones as an alternate fuel. Adequate carbohydrate spares protein from being used this way. Fiber cannot be converted into usable glucose, and fatty acids cannot be converted directly into glucose, so those options are wrong; glucose-dependent tissues like the brain still need fuel.
rationales.eli10: If the sugar (glucose) runs low, your body does not just give up, it improvises. It tears down some protein to build new glucose, and it starts burning fat in a special way that makes backup fuel called ketones. Eating enough carbs means your body does not have to raid its protein to keep going, which is called protein sparing.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: When carbohydrate is severely limited, the body makes glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as amino acids (gluconeogenesis) to protect essential glucose-dependent tissues, and it increases fat breakdown, producing ketones as an alternate fuel. Adequate carbohydrate spares protein from being used this way. Fiber cannot be converted into usable glucose, and fatty acids cannot be converted directly into glucose, so those options are wrong; glucose-dependent tissues like the brain still need fuel.

questions.stem: The Dietary Guidelines for Americans advise minimizing added sugars while encouraging fiber-rich whole grains and fruit. Which reasoning best explains why these two carbohydrate sources are treated differently?

options.text: Added sugars contain no calories of their own, while whole grains and fruit are the only true energy sources
Added sugars supply energy with few other nutrients, while whole grains and fruit add fiber and vitamins
Whole grains and fruit are the simple sugars, while added sugars are slow-releasing complex carbohydrates
Added sugars are digested more slowly than starch and therefore cause smaller, more gradual glucose spikes

rationales.whyCorrect: Option B is correct because added sugars provide energy but little accompanying nutrition, often described as empty calories. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030 state that no amount of added sugars is recommended or considered part of a healthy diet, and offer the practical benchmark that one meal should contain no more than 10 grams of added sugars. By contrast, the same guidelines tell people to prioritize fiber-rich whole grains and to eat a variety of fruits, because those foods deliver carbohydrate together with fiber, vitamins, and minerals, giving greater nutrient value per calorie. The distinction is about nutrient density, not calorie content, sugar classification, or digestion speed. A is wrong because added sugars do supply calories, about 4 kcal per gram, the same as any other digestible carbohydrate, and they are certainly not the only energy source. C reverses the chemistry: added sugars are the simple sugars, while whole grains supply starch, a complex carbohydrate, and added sugars are not slow-releasing. D reverses the physiology: added sugars, especially in beverages, are absorbed rapidly and raise blood glucose faster than the fiber-containing carbohydrate in whole grains and whole fruit.
rationales.eli10: Two foods can both give you energy, but one comes with a bonus and one comes empty-handed. Fruit and whole grains bring their carbs plus fiber and vitamins, like a gift that has extra presents packed inside. Added sugars bring pretty much just the energy and no bonus, which is why they are called empty calories and why the nutrition guidelines say to keep them to a minimum instead of making them part of your regular meals.

questions.stem: Which comparison of glycogen and starch is accurate?

options.text: Both are simple sugars built from fructose, but glycogen is found in plants and starch is found in animals
Glycogen is a plant fiber that humans cannot digest, while starch passes through the gut fully indigestible
Both are storage polysaccharides of glucose, but glycogen is stored in animals and starch in plants
Starch is a single sugar unit like glucose, while glycogen is a two-unit disaccharide like sucrose

rationales.whyCorrect: Both starch and glycogen are polysaccharides made of many glucose units linked together, and both serve as glucose storage. Starch is the storage form in plants (grains, potatoes), while glycogen is the storage form in animals (liver and muscle). A is wrong on both counts: neither is a simple sugar, neither is built from fructose, and the plant/animal locations are reversed. B is wrong because glycogen is an animal polysaccharide, not a plant fiber, and starch is readily digested by amylase rather than passing through intact. D is wrong because starch is not a single sugar unit and glycogen is not a disaccharide; both are large, many-unit polysaccharides.
rationales.eli10: Starch and glycogen are basically the same idea, a big bundle of glucose beads saved for later, but they live in different places. Plants stash their glucose as starch, and animals (including you) stash it as glycogen. Same job, different address.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Both starch and glycogen are polysaccharides made of many glucose units linked together, and both serve as glucose storage. Starch is the storage form in plants (grains, potatoes), while glycogen is the storage form in animals (liver and muscle). A is wrong on both counts: neither is a simple sugar, neither is built from fructose, and the plant/animal locations are reversed. B is wrong because glycogen is an animal polysaccharide, not a plant fiber, and starch is readily digested by amylase rather than passing through intact. D is wrong because starch is not a single sugar unit and glycogen is not a disaccharide; both are large, many-unit polysaccharides.

questions.stem: Which term describes the basic building-block molecules that link together to form dietary proteins?

rationales.whyCorrect: Proteins are polymers built from amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Fatty acids are the building blocks of fats, monosaccharides of carbohydrates, and nucleotides of nucleic acids. Recognizing amino acids as the protein subunit is the foundation for understanding protein digestion, synthesis, and nutritional quality.
rationales.eli10: Think of a protein like a beaded necklace. Each little bead is an amino acid, and stringing many beads together makes the whole necklace, which is the protein. Fats and carbs use different kinds of beads, so amino acids are the special beads just for proteins.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Proteins are polymers built from amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Fatty acids are the building blocks of fats, monosaccharides of carbohydrates, and nucleotides of nucleic acids. Recognizing amino acids as the protein subunit is the foundation for understanding protein digestion, synthesis, and nutritional quality.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines an essential amino acid?

options.text: An amino acid the body can synthesize in adequate amounts from other compounds
An amino acid the body uses only to build muscle tissue, not enzymes or hormones
An amino acid the body cannot make in adequate amounts and must be eaten
An amino acid supplied only by animal foods and never by plant sources

rationales.whyCorrect: Essential (indispensable) amino acids cannot be made by the body in sufficient quantities, so they must be supplied by food (C). Nonessential amino acids are the ones the body can synthesize from other compounds (A). Amino acids build enzymes, hormones, and transport proteins as well as muscle (B), and essential amino acids occur in plant foods such as soy, beans, and grains, not only in animal foods (D).
rationales.eli10: Your body is like a kitchen that can cook some ingredients by itself but not others. The ones it can't make have to be bought at the store, which here means eaten in food. Those store-bought-only ingredients are the essential amino acids.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Essential (indispensable) amino acids cannot be made by the body in sufficient quantities, so they must be supplied by food (C). Nonessential amino acids are the ones the body can synthesize from other compounds (A). Amino acids build enzymes, hormones, and transport proteins as well as muscle (B), and essential amino acids occur in plant foods such as soy, beans, and grains, not only in animal foods (D).

questions.stem: Which term describes a food that supplies all nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions?

rationales.whyCorrect: A complete (high-quality) protein contains all nine essential amino acids in amounts that meet human needs; most animal foods and soy qualify. Incomplete proteins are low in one or more essential amino acids, complementary proteins are combinations that together supply all essentials, and the limiting amino acid is the one in shortest supply.
rationales.eli10: Imagine you need all nine puzzle pieces to finish a picture. A complete protein hands you the whole set in one box. If a food is missing a piece or two, it isn't complete, and you'd have to grab the missing pieces from another food.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A complete (high-quality) protein contains all nine essential amino acids in amounts that meet human needs; most animal foods and soy qualify. Incomplete proteins are low in one or more essential amino acids, complementary proteins are combinations that together supply all essentials, and the limiting amino acid is the one in shortest supply.

questions.stem: What is the primary reason peptide bonds must be broken during protein digestion?

options.text: To convert dietary protein directly into glucose for immediate energy
To free individual amino acids small enough to be absorbed by the body
To remove the nitrogen from food proteins before they enter the stomach
To transform amino acids into fatty acids for long-term fat storage

rationales.whyCorrect: Dietary proteins are too large to cross the intestinal lining intact, so digestive enzymes break peptide bonds and free amino acids (and small peptides) for absorption and reuse in the body's own proteins (B). Digestion is not aimed at making glucose (A) or fat (D), and nitrogen is not stripped from food before it reaches the stomach (C).
rationales.eli10: The necklace of amino acids is too big to fit through the tiny doors in your gut wall. Digestion snips the string between the beads so each single bead can slip through the door and get used to build brand-new necklaces your body needs.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Dietary proteins are too large to cross the intestinal lining intact, so digestive enzymes break peptide bonds and free amino acids (and small peptides) for absorption and reuse in the body's own proteins (B). Digestion is not aimed at making glucose (A) or fat (D), and nitrogen is not stripped from food before it reaches the stomach (C).

questions.stem: Which comparison between animal and most plant protein sources is accurate?

options.text: Most plant proteins are complete, while animal proteins are usually incomplete
Animal and plant proteins are always limited in the same essential amino acid
Most animal proteins are complete, while many single plant proteins are not
Animal proteins contain several amino acids that plant proteins never contain

rationales.whyCorrect: Most animal foods (and soy) supply all nine essential amino acids in adequate amounts, while many individual plant foods fall short in a particular one, such as lysine in grains or methionine in legumes (C). Option A reverses this. The limiting amino acid differs from food to food rather than being the same in every protein (B), and plant and animal foods contain the same set of amino acids, differing only in proportion (D).
rationales.eli10: Animal foods usually bring the whole set of puzzle pieces. A single plant food often shows up short one piece, but a different plant has extra of that piece, so mixing plants fills in what's missing. Same pieces overall, just spread out differently.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Most animal foods (and soy) supply all nine essential amino acids in adequate amounts, while many individual plant foods fall short in a particular one, such as lysine in grains or methionine in legumes (C). Option A reverses this. The limiting amino acid differs from food to food rather than being the same in every protein (B), and plant and animal foods contain the same set of amino acids, differing only in proportion (D).

questions.stem: Which example correctly illustrates complementary proteins?

options.text: Eating grilled chicken with a glass of milk
Eating an egg with a slice of cheese
Eating salmon with a side of yogurt

rationales.whyCorrect: Complementary proteins are two incomplete plant proteins whose amino acid profiles fill each other's gaps: legumes are low in methionine but rich in lysine, while grains are low in lysine but supply methionine. Together beans and rice provide all essential amino acids. The other pairs combine complete animal proteins, which do not need complementing.
rationales.eli10: Beans are missing one puzzle piece and rice is missing a different one. Eat both and each one hands over the piece the other lacks, so together they make a full picture. They don't even have to be at the same meal, since beans at lunch and rice at dinner works too because your body pools the pieces across the day. That teamwork is what complementary proteins means.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Complementary proteins are two incomplete plant proteins whose amino acid profiles fill each other's gaps: legumes are low in methionine but rich in lysine, while grains are low in lysine but supply methionine. Together beans and rice provide all essential amino acids. The other pairs combine complete animal proteins, which do not need complementing.

questions.stem: Which change would most likely occur if a person's diet supplied enough total protein but was low in one essential amino acid?

options.text: Protein synthesis would be limited by the amino acid in shortest supply
Protein synthesis would proceed normally because the body stores extra amino acids
The body would convert fat into the missing amino acid
The missing amino acid would be replaced automatically by a nonessential one

rationales.whyCorrect: Building a protein requires all needed amino acids to be present simultaneously; when the limiting amino acid runs out, synthesis of that protein stalls even if other amino acids are abundant. The body does not maintain a dedicated amino acid store, cannot make essential amino acids from fat, and cannot substitute a nonessential amino acid for an essential one.
rationales.eli10: To build a toy car you need four wheels. If you have hundreds of every other part but only three wheels, you can only finish as many cars as your wheels allow. The part you run out of first, the limiting amino acid, decides how much you can build.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Building a protein requires all needed amino acids to be present simultaneously; when the limiting amino acid runs out, synthesis of that protein stalls even if other amino acids are abundant. The body does not maintain a dedicated amino acid store, cannot make essential amino acids from fat, and cannot substitute a nonessential amino acid for an essential one.

questions.stem: During a period of very low calorie intake, the body begins breaking down muscle protein for fuel. Which explanation best accounts for this?

options.text: Protein is the body's preferred fuel, burned ahead of carbohydrate and fat
Excess dietary protein is reliably stored as new muscle tissue for later use
Muscle protein cannot be broken down for energy under any dietary condition
Inadequate carbohydrate and fat intake forces the body to burn body protein

rationales.whyCorrect: Carbohydrate and fat are the body's main fuels and spare protein for its structural and functional roles; when energy intake is too low, the body catabolizes muscle protein and uses certain amino acids for gluconeogenesis (D). Protein is not the preferred first fuel (A), surplus amino acids are not warehoused as muscle (B), and muscle protein clearly can be broken down for energy, which is exactly what happens here (C).
rationales.eli10: Your body likes to burn carbs and fat for energy, like using firewood. When the firewood runs out, it starts burning the furniture, meaning your muscles, just to stay warm. Eating enough calories keeps the furniture safe so muscle isn't wasted.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Carbohydrate and fat are the body's main fuels and spare protein for its structural and functional roles; when energy intake is too low, the body catabolizes muscle protein and uses certain amino acids for gluconeogenesis (D). Protein is not the preferred first fuel (A), surplus amino acids are not warehoused as muscle (B), and muscle protein clearly can be broken down for energy, which is exactly what happens here (C).

A limiting protein because it lists a specific gram amount
A complementary protein that must be paired with another food

questions.stem: Because the body has no dedicated storage form for amino acids, what typically happens to amino acids eaten well beyond the body's protein needs?

options.text: Their nitrogen leaves the body as urea, while the rest is burned or stored as fat
They are stored intact in liver and muscle depots for later use in protein synthesis
They are absorbed intact and then excreted unchanged in the urine as whole amino acids
They are automatically converted into whichever essential amino acids the diet lacks

rationales.whyCorrect: Surplus amino acids are deaminated in the liver: the nitrogen-containing amino group becomes urea and is excreted by the kidneys, while the remaining carbon skeleton is oxidized for energy or converted to fat for storage (A). There is no storage depot that holds amino acids intact (B), amino acids are not excreted whole in the urine (C), and the body cannot manufacture essential amino acids from other amino acids (D).
rationales.eli10: Your body can't keep leftover amino acids in a pantry for later. When you eat more protein than you need, it strips off the nitrogen part, which leaves the body as urea in urine, and then burns or stores the rest, often as fat. So extra protein doesn't simply pile up as muscle.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Surplus amino acids are deaminated in the liver: the nitrogen-containing amino group becomes urea and is excreted by the kidneys, while the remaining carbon skeleton is oxidized for energy or converted to fat for storage (A). There is no storage depot that holds amino acids intact (B), amino acids are not excreted whole in the urine (C), and the body cannot manufacture essential amino acids from other amino acids (D).

questions.stem: Which comparison between essential and nonessential amino acids is accurate?

options.text: Nonessential amino acids are unimportant and can be left out of the body's proteins
Nonessential amino acids must always be eaten, while essential ones are made by the body
Essential amino acids are needed for muscle, while nonessential ones are used only for enzymes

questions.stem: Which statement correctly identifies a saturated fatty acid?

options.text: It contains one carbon-to-carbon double bond in its chain
It contains two or more carbon-to-carbon double bonds in its chain
It has no carbon-to-carbon double bonds and is filled with hydrogen
It has been chemically converted from a liquid oil using nitrogen

rationales.whyCorrect: A saturated fatty acid has only single bonds between its carbons, so every carbon holds the maximum number of hydrogen atoms — it is 'saturated' with hydrogen, which is what option C states. Option A describes a monounsaturated fatty acid (exactly one carbon-to-carbon double bond) and option B a polyunsaturated fatty acid (two or more). Option D fails on two counts: the industrial process that hardens a liquid oil adds hydrogen gas over a metal catalyst, not nitrogen, and saturation is defined by the molecule's structure, not by how the fat was manufactured. Fully hydrogenating an oil does saturate it, because hydrogen is added across every double bond; partial hydrogenation instead leaves some double bonds in place and converts part of them from the cis to the trans configuration, which is how industrial trans fat is formed.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a school bus where every seat is filled with a kid (hydrogen). A saturated fat is a full bus — no empty seats, all single connections. When there are empty seats (double bonds), the fat is unsaturated instead. Factories can fill those empty seats by adding hydrogen, but that is a way of making a fat, not the definition of one.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A saturated fatty acid has only single bonds between its carbons, so every carbon holds the maximum number of hydrogen atoms — it is 'saturated' with hydrogen, which is what option C states. questions.stem: At room temperature, which physical property is most typical of fats high in saturated fatty acids compared with fats high in unsaturated fatty acids?

options.text: They are usually liquid rather than solid
They are usually solid rather than liquid
They contain no calories per gram

rationales.whyCorrect: Saturated fatty acids have straight chains that pack tightly together, so saturated fats such as butter and lard tend to be solid at room temperature. Unsaturated fats have kinked chains from their double bonds and stay liquid as oils; all fats provide about 9 kcal/g, and fats are not water-soluble.
rationales.eli10: Straight uncooked spaghetti stacks neatly into a tight solid pile, but bent noodles can't stack and stay loose. Saturated fats are the straight noodles (solid, like butter), and unsaturated fats are the bent ones (liquid, like olive oil).

questions.stem: What is the primary reason essential fatty acids such as linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid must be obtained from the diet?

options.text: They provide more energy per gram than any other nutrient in the body
The body lacks the enzymes to place double bonds at those specific positions in the chain
The body destroys them during digestion and must constantly replace them
They are the only fatty acids the liver can store for long periods

rationales.whyCorrect: Linoleic (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic (omega-3) acids are essential because humans lack the desaturase enzymes needed to insert double bonds beyond the ninth carbon (counting from the carboxyl, or acid, end) — precisely the omega-6 and omega-3 positions — so these fatty acids must come from food. They are needed for cell membranes and to make signaling compounds, and the fact that they cannot be made internally, not their energy content or storage, is what makes them dietary essentials.
rationales.eli10: Your body is like a factory that can build most fat parts but is missing the specific tool needed to add a bend at one far end of the chain. Since it can't make that bend itself, you have to get those already-bent fats (from foods like fish and seeds) delivered ready-made.

questions.stem: Which comparison between LDL and HDL cholesterol is accurate?

options.text: HDL carries cholesterol toward tissues and arteries, while LDL returns it to the liver
LDL carries cholesterol toward tissues and arteries, while HDL helps return cholesterol to the liver
LDL and HDL are types of dietary fiber that trap cholesterol in the gut
Both LDL and HDL are enzymes that break cholesterol into fatty acids

rationales.whyCorrect: Lipoproteins transport water-insoluble cholesterol through the blood; LDL (low-density lipoprotein) delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues and, in excess, contributes to arterial plaque, while HDL (high-density lipoprotein) carries cholesterol back to the liver for removal. This is why LDL is often called 'bad' and HDL 'good'; they are transport particles, not fiber or enzymes.
rationales.eli10: Picture delivery trucks in your blood. LDL trucks drop cholesterol off around the body, and if too many pile up they clog the roads (arteries). HDL trucks pick cholesterol back up and haul it to the liver for cleanup — that's why HDL is the helpful one.

questions.stem: Which change in food processing most directly explains how a liquid vegetable oil becomes a solid, shelf-stable fat that contains trans fatty acids?

rationales.whyCorrect: Partial hydrogenation adds hydrogen to some double bonds of an unsaturated oil, making it more solid and resistant to spoilage, but the process also converts some remaining double bonds from the natural cis configuration to the trans configuration. questions.stem: A person examines an older packaged food whose Nutrition Facts label shows 0 g trans fat, but sees 'partially hydrogenated oil' in the ingredient list. What is the most accurate interpretation?

options.text: The food may contain a trace of trans fat below the rounding cutoff
The ingredient list is outdated and the food is truly trans-fat free
Partially hydrogenated oil is a plant-derived omega-3 fatty acid
The food must contain more than 5 g of trans fat hidden by the label

rationales.whyCorrect: U.S. labeling rules allow a product with less than 0.5 g of trans fat per serving to be declared as 0 g, so 'partially hydrogenated oil' in the ingredient list signals that a trace of trans fat may still be present. This teaches students to read the ingredient list, not just the rounded number. B is wrong because the ingredient list is the more reliable clue here, not an outdated error, and the food is not truly trans-fat free; C is wrong because partially hydrogenated oil is an industrially processed fat, not an omega-3; D is wrong because the rounding rule caps the undeclared amount at just under 0.5 g per serving, nowhere near 5 g. Note that the scenario is historical: FDA revoked the 'generally recognized as safe' status of partially hydrogenated oils in 2015, and foods containing them could no longer be distributed in the United States after January 1, 2021, so that ingredient would appear only on an older or non-U.S. label. The same rounding rule still applies today to small amounts of residual or naturally occurring (ruminant) trans fat, so a '0 g' declaration still does not guarantee literally zero.
rationales.eli10: The label can round tiny amounts down to zero, like saying you have 'zero dollars' when you actually have a few coins. On an older package, seeing 'partially hydrogenated oil' in the ingredients was the clue that a little trans fat may still be hiding in there. It does not mean the ingredient list is out of date, that the oil is a healthy omega-3, or that a huge hidden amount is in there, because the rounding rule only hides amounts under half a gram per serving. Foods sold in the U.S. today no longer use that ingredient, but the rounding rule is the same, so '0 g' can still mean 'a very small amount' rather than none at all.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen to the absorption of vitamins A, D, E, and K if a person followed an extremely low-fat diet over a long period?

options.text: These vitamins would be converted into fatty acids for storage
Absorption of these vitamins would increase because less fat competes for space
These vitamins would be absorbed normally because they dissolve in water
Absorption of these vitamins would likely decrease because dietary fat aids their uptake

rationales.whyCorrect: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble, so their digestion and absorption depend on the presence of dietary fat and the bile it triggers to form absorbable micelles. A chronically very-low-fat diet can therefore impair uptake of these vitamins; they do not dissolve in water and are not converted into fatty acids.
rationales.eli10: Fat-soluble vitamins are like passengers who can only cross a river by riding in a fat 'boat.' Take away almost all the fat and there are few boats, so the vitamins get stranded and don't make it into the body as well.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble, so their digestion and absorption depend on the presence of dietary fat and the bile it triggers to form absorbable micelles. A chronically very-low-fat diet can therefore impair uptake of these vitamins; they do not dissolve in water and are not converted into fatty acids.

questions.stem: Two fats provide the same number of grams and therefore the same calories, but one is rich in omega-3 polyunsaturated fat and the other is rich in trans fat. Which comparison of their likely effects on blood lipids is accurate?

options.text: Both raise LDL and lower HDL to the same degree because their calorie contents are equal
The omega-3 fat raises LDL much more than the trans fat does at equal calories
The trans fat raises LDL and lowers HDL, while the omega-3 fat is more favorable
Neither one affects blood lipids at all because both are simply dietary fats

rationales.whyCorrect: Even at identical calories, the type of fat matters: industrial trans fat characteristically raises LDL and lowers HDL, an unfavorable pattern, whereas omega-3 polyunsaturated fats support a more favorable lipid profile and cardiovascular health. This shows that fat quality, not just quantity or calories, drives the effect on blood lipids.
rationales.eli10: Same amount of energy doesn't mean same effect on your body. The trans fat pushes the 'bad' cholesterol up and the 'good' one down, while the omega-3 fat treats your blood vessels kindly — so the kind of fat matters, not just how many calories.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Even at identical calories, the type of fat matters: industrial trans fat characteristically raises LDL and lowers HDL, an unfavorable pattern, whereas omega-3 polyunsaturated fats support a more favorable lipid profile and cardiovascular health. This shows that fat quality, not just quantity or calories, drives the effect on blood lipids.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines a vitamin?

options.text: A macronutrient that the body burns to supply most of its daily energy
An inorganic element, such as iron or calcium, that the body uses to build its tissues
An organic compound needed in small amounts for normal metabolism, usually obtained from the diet
A form of dietary fiber that passes through the gut without being digested

rationales.whyCorrect: Vitamins are organic (carbon-containing) micronutrients required in small quantities to support metabolic processes, and because the body cannot synthesize most of them in adequate amounts, they must come from food. This distinguishes them from minerals, which are inorganic, and from macronutrients, which supply energy in large amounts.
rationales.eli10: Think of vitamins as tiny helper tools your body needs to get its jobs done. You only need a little bit of each, but you have to get them from food because your body can't make enough on its own. They are 'organic,' meaning they come from living things like plants and animals, unlike minerals, which come from rocks and soil.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Vitamins are organic (carbon-containing) micronutrients required in small quantities to support metabolic processes, and because the body cannot synthesize most of them in adequate amounts, they must come from food. questions.stem: Vitamins are commonly divided into two main groups based on what property?

options.text: Whether they provide energy or not
Whether they come from plants or from animals
Whether they dissolve in fat or in water
Whether they are found in raw or cooked foods

rationales.whyCorrect: The standard classification of vitamins is fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) versus water-soluble (the B-complex vitamins and vitamin C). Solubility determines how a vitamin is absorbed, transported, and stored, making it the defining property for grouping them.
rationales.eli10: Vitamins get sorted into two clubs based on what they can dissolve in, like sugar dissolving in water but oil not mixing with it. Some vitamins dissolve in fat and some dissolve in water. This matters a lot because it changes how your body stores them and how easily you can get too much or too little.

questions.stem: Which group correctly lists the four fat-soluble vitamins?

options.text: Vitamins A, D, E, and K
Vitamins B6, B12, C, and D
Vitamins A, C, E, and K
Vitamins B1, B2, B3, and C

rationales.whyCorrect: The four fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, and K; a common memory aid is the mnemonic 'ADEK.' All other vitamins (the B-complex and vitamin C) are water-soluble, so any list containing C or a B vitamin among the fat-soluble group is incorrect.
rationales.eli10: An easy way to remember the fat-soluble vitamins is the word ADEK, like a name. Those four ride around your body in fat. Vitamin C and all the B vitamins are the water-loving ones, so if you see a C or a B in the list, it does not belong in the fat club.

questions.stem: Why can fat-soluble vitamins build up to toxic levels more easily than water-soluble vitamins?

options.text: They are absorbed much faster from the stomach than water-soluble vitamins
They are stored in the liver and fatty tissue rather than being readily excreted in urine
The body converts them into minerals that cannot be broken down
They are chemically stronger and resist digestion in the intestine

rationales.whyCorrect: Because fat-soluble vitamins are stored in body fat and the liver, excess amounts accumulate over time instead of being flushed out. Water-soluble vitamins, in contrast, are largely excreted in the urine when intake exceeds needs, so they rarely reach toxic levels. This storage difference is why excess vitamin A and vitamin D in particular, usually from supplements, can build up and cause harm. Vitamin K is the exception among the fat-soluble vitamins: it turns over rapidly and has no established tolerable upper intake level because of its low potential for toxicity.
rationales.eli10: Water-soluble vitamins are like water in a cup with a hole in the bottom, extra just drains out in your pee. Fat-soluble vitamins are more like putting stuff in a closet, they get stored away and pile up. If you keep stuffing the closet, it can overflow and cause problems, which is why too much vitamin A or vitamin D, usually from supplement pills, can actually make you sick.

questions.stem: Many B vitamins share which primary role in the body?

options.text: Carrying oxygen from the lungs to working muscles and other body tissues
Serving as the main structural building blocks of bone and tooth enamel
Acting as coenzymes that help enzymes release energy from digested food
Providing a direct source of calories that muscles burn during contraction

rationales.whyCorrect: B-complex vitamins function chiefly as coenzymes in the metabolic pathways that release energy from digested carbohydrate, fat, and protein. They do not themselves supply calories (option D); oxygen transport belongs to the iron in hemoglobin, not to B vitamins (option A); and the structural framework of bone and teeth is built from calcium and phosphorus, not B vitamins (option B). This coenzyme role is why B-vitamin deficiencies often produce fatigue and impaired energy metabolism.
rationales.eli10: B vitamins are like the little keys that turn on the machines in your body that unlock energy from food. The food is the fuel, but without the keys the machines can't run. That is why B vitamins are called coenzymes, they team up with your body's workers (enzymes) to get energy out of what you eat.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: B-complex vitamins function chiefly as coenzymes in the metabolic pathways that release energy from digested carbohydrate, fat, and protein. They do not themselves supply calories (option D); oxygen transport belongs to the iron in hemoglobin, not to B vitamins (option A); and the structural framework of bone and teeth is built from calcium and phosphorus, not B vitamins (option B). This coenzyme role is why B-vitamin deficiencies often produce fatigue and impaired energy metabolism.

questions.stem: Which comparison between vitamin D and most other vitamins is accurate?

options.text: Vitamin D cannot be stored in the liver, while most other vitamins can be
Vitamin D supplies four calories per gram, while other vitamins supply none
Vitamin D is water-soluble and lost in urine, while most vitamins are not
Vitamin D is made in the skin from sunlight, while most vitamins are not

rationales.whyCorrect: Vitamin D is unusual because the body synthesizes it when skin is exposed to ultraviolet light, so it is sometimes called the 'sunshine vitamin.' Most vitamins must be obtained from food because the body cannot produce them in adequate amounts. Option A is wrong because vitamin D is fat-soluble and is readily stored in the liver and fatty tissue. Option C fails for the same reason: vitamin D is not water-soluble and is not flushed out in urine the way vitamin C and the B vitamins are. Option B is wrong because no vitamin, including D, supplies calories; energy comes only from carbohydrate, fat, protein, and alcohol.
rationales.eli10: Most vitamins are like groceries, you have to go get them from food. But vitamin D is special because your skin can actually build it when sunlight hits you, kind of like a tiny solar panel. That is why people call it the sunshine vitamin, and why you can run low on it in dark winter months.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if a person's diet lacked vitamin C over a long period?

options.text: Night vision would deteriorate and the surface of the eyes would become very dry
Blood would fail to clot after minor cuts because clotting factors could not be formed
The body would lose the ability to absorb calcium, and the bones would gradually soften
Collagen formation would be impaired, causing weak connective tissue, bleeding gums, and poor wound healing

rationales.whyCorrect: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is the cofactor for the prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes that stabilize collagen, the protein that gives strength to skin, blood vessels, gums, and other connective tissue. Prolonged deficiency causes scurvy, marked by bleeding gums, easy bruising, and poor wound healing. Each distractor describes a different vitamin's deficiency: option A (night blindness and dry eyes, or xerophthalmia) is vitamin A deficiency; option B (clotting factors cannot be formed) is vitamin K deficiency, because vitamin K is required to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X; option C (calcium is not absorbed and bones soften) is vitamin D deficiency, seen as rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
rationales.eli10: Vitamin C is like the glue that holds your body's building materials together, especially the stuff called collagen in your skin and gums. Without enough glue, things start falling apart, gums bleed, cuts don't heal, and you bruise easily. That old sailor's disease called scurvy happened because they had no fresh fruit and ran out of vitamin C. The other choices are what happens when a different vitamin runs out: vitamin A keeps your night vision and eyes moist, vitamin K helps blood form scabs, and vitamin D helps you absorb calcium so bones stay hard.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is the cofactor for the prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes that stabilize collagen, the protein that gives strength to skin, blood vessels, gums, and other connective tissue. Prolonged deficiency causes scurvy, marked by bleeding gums, easy bruising, and poor wound healing. Each distractor describes a different vitamin's deficiency: option A (night blindness and dry eyes, or xerophthalmia) is vitamin A deficiency; option B (clotting factors cannot be formed) is vitamin K deficiency, because vitamin K is required to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X; option C (calcium is not absorbed and bones soften) is vitamin D deficiency, seen as rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

questions.stem: A nutrition student wants to increase dietary vitamin A from a plant source. Which food choice would best meet that goal?

options.text: Citrus fruits such as oranges and grapefruit
Carrots and sweet potatoes, which are rich in beta-carotene

rationales.whyCorrect: Orange and deep-yellow plant foods like carrots and sweet potatoes contain beta-carotene, a provitamin the body converts to vitamin A. Citrus fruits are known for vitamin C, whole grains for B vitamins, and nuts and vegetable oils for vitamin E, so those choices would not primarily boost vitamin A intake.
rationales.eli10: That bright orange color in carrots and sweet potatoes comes from beta-carotene, which your body turns into vitamin A. So if you want more vitamin A from plants, reach for the orange veggies. Oranges give you vitamin C instead, and nuts give you vitamin E, so color and food type are good clues.

questions.stem: Which cooking or storage practice would most likely reduce the vitamin C content of vegetables?

options.text: Boiling them for a long time in a large amount of water
Storing them briefly in a cool, dark refrigerator
Eating them raw shortly after purchase
Steaming them quickly over a small amount of water

rationales.whyCorrect: Vitamin C is water-soluble and heat-sensitive, so prolonged boiling causes it to leach into the cooking water and to be destroyed by heat and oxygen. Quick steaming, refrigeration, and eating vegetables raw all help preserve vitamin C, making boiling the practice most likely to reduce it.
rationales.eli10: Vitamin C is a fragile, water-loving vitamin, so when you boil veggies for a long time it escapes into the water and gets wrecked by the heat. It is like washing colored chalk in a bucket, the color runs out into the water. Quick steaming or eating them raw keeps more of the vitamin inside the food.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Vitamin C is water-soluble and heat-sensitive, so prolonged boiling causes it to leach into the cooking water and to be destroyed by heat and oxygen. Quick steaming, refrigeration, and eating vegetables raw all help preserve vitamin C, making boiling the practice most likely to reduce it.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman is advised to get adequate folate (vitamin B9). What is the primary purpose of this recommendation?

options.text: To support proper formation of the baby's neural tube and lower the risk of birth defects
To strengthen the mother's bones by improving her absorption of dietary calcium
To improve the mother's night vision during the later stages of pregnancy
To help the mother's blood clot properly during labor and delivery

rationales.whyCorrect: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and rapid cell division, and adequate intake around conception and early pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida. This is why folic acid supplementation is recommended for women who may become pregnant. Calcium absorption relates to vitamin D, night vision to vitamin A, and clotting to vitamin K.
rationales.eli10: When a baby is growing, its cells are dividing super fast, and folate is the vitamin that helps build brand-new cells and DNA correctly. Early on, the baby's brain and spine (the neural tube) form, and enough folate helps that happen without mistakes. That is why doctors want moms to get plenty of folate before and during early pregnancy.

questions.stem: A strict vegan who eats no animal products at all is at greatest risk for deficiency of which vitamin, and why?

options.text: Vitamin C, because plant foods contain very little of it
Vitamin B12, because it is found almost exclusively in animal-derived foods
Vitamin E, because it is destroyed during the digestion of plant foods
Vitamin K, because it is only produced by animal tissue

rationales.whyCorrect: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) occurs naturally almost only in animal products such as meat, fish, eggs, and dairy, so people avoiding all animal foods need fortified foods or supplements to prevent deficiency, which can cause anemia and nerve damage. Vitamin C is abundant in plants, vitamin E is found in plant oils and nuts, and vitamin K is plentiful in leafy greens, so those are not the primary vegan concern.
rationales.eli10: Most vitamins hide in plenty of plant foods, but vitamin B12 is the tricky one, it comes almost entirely from animal foods like meat, eggs, and milk. So someone eating only plants can slowly run out unless they take a supplement or eat foods with B12 added. Without it, your blood and nerves start having trouble.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) occurs naturally almost only in animal products such as meat, fish, eggs, and dairy, so people avoiding all animal foods need fortified foods or supplements to prevent deficiency, which can cause anemia and nerve damage. Vitamin C is abundant in plants, vitamin E is found in plant oils and nuts, and vitamin K is plentiful in leafy greens, so those are not the primary vegan concern.

questions.stem: A patient on a long-term antibiotic that suppresses gut bacteria and who eats few leafy greens develops easy bruising and slow blood clotting. A deficiency of which vitamin best explains this, and why?

options.text: Vitamin A, because it maintains the smooth lining of the body's blood vessels
Vitamin K, because it makes clotting factors and comes partly from gut bacteria and greens
Vitamin B12, because it is required to produce platelets within the bone marrow
Vitamin E, because it keeps red blood cell membranes from rupturing easily

rationales.whyCorrect: Vitamin K is essential for synthesizing several blood-clotting factors, and it comes both from dietary sources like leafy green vegetables and from synthesis by gut bacteria. Antibiotics that suppress those bacteria, combined with low dietary intake, can lower vitamin K status and impair clotting, producing easy bruising and prolonged bleeding. The other vitamins are not the primary drivers of clotting-factor production.
rationales.eli10: Vitamin K is the vitamin your body uses to make blood clot and stop bleeding, like the tools that seal a leak. You get it from leafy greens and also from helpful bacteria living in your gut. If antibiotics wipe out those bacteria and you don't eat greens, you run short, and cuts bleed longer and bruises appear easily.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Vitamin K is essential for synthesizing several blood-clotting factors, and it comes both from dietary sources like leafy green vegetables and from synthesis by gut bacteria. Antibiotics that suppress those bacteria, combined with low dietary intake, can lower vitamin K status and impair clotting, producing easy bruising and prolonged bleeding. The other vitamins are not the primary drivers of clotting-factor production.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines a dietary mineral?

options.text: An organic compound the body builds from amino acids
An inorganic element obtained from food that the body cannot make
A type of vitamin that dissolves only in fat
A carbohydrate the body stores for quick energy

rationales.whyCorrect: Minerals are inorganic elements (such as calcium, iron, and sodium) that plants and animals cannot synthesize, so they must be supplied through the diet. Unlike vitamins, they are not carbon-based organic molecules and cannot be destroyed by heat or light. This distinction is why mineral intake depends on the mineral content of soil, water, and food.
rationales.eli10: Think of minerals like little building blocks that come from the earth, not something your body can build in its own kitchen. Vitamins are made of stuff living things put together, but minerals are simple earth-elements like iron and calcium. Since your body has no factory to make them, you have to eat them.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Minerals are inorganic elements (such as calcium, iron, and sodium) that plants and animals cannot synthesize, so they must be supplied through the diet. questions.stem: Which term describes minerals such as iron, zinc, and iodine that the body needs in amounts of less than 100 milligrams per day?

rationales.whyCorrect: Trace minerals (microminerals) such as iron, zinc, iodine, and selenium are required in very small amounts, generally under 100 mg per day, yet remain essential for health. Major minerals like calcium and phosphorus are needed in larger amounts, electrolytes are defined by their charge rather than their required amount, and 'fat-soluble' describes certain vitamins, not minerals. Being needed in small quantities does not make trace minerals less important.
rationales.eli10: Some minerals your body needs by the spoonful, and some it needs by just a tiny pinch. The tiny-pinch ones are called trace minerals, like iron and zinc. 'Trace' means only a little, but even a little is really important, like a pinch of salt that changes a whole recipe.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the primary electrolyte found in fluid outside the body's cells?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sodium is the major cation of the extracellular fluid and is the main determinant of extracellular fluid volume and osmolarity. Potassium, by contrast, is the primary intracellular cation. This division of sodium outside and potassium inside cells is central to fluid balance and nerve function.
rationales.eli10: Imagine each cell is a tiny water balloon. Sodium mostly floats in the water around the balloons, while potassium mostly stays inside them. Because sodium is the boss of the water outside, it decides how much water hangs around your cells.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Sodium is the major cation of the extracellular fluid and is the main determinant of extracellular fluid volume and osmolarity. Potassium, by contrast, is the primary intracellular cation. This division of sodium outside and potassium inside cells is central to fluid balance and nerve function.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of electrolytes such as sodium and potassium in the body?

options.text: To carry electrical charges for nerve signals and fluid balance
To build the protein framework of muscle fibers and tendons
To supply four calories per gram for use as cellular energy
To act as antioxidants that neutralize free radicals inside cells

rationales.whyCorrect: Electrolytes are minerals that dissociate into charged ions in body fluids, allowing them to conduct electrical signals needed for nerve transmission and muscle contraction while regulating the distribution of water across cell membranes. They supply no calories at all, since minerals are not energy-yielding nutrients; the protein framework of muscle and tendon is built from amino acids, not from sodium or potassium; and antioxidant defense belongs to compounds such as vitamins C and E and selenium-containing enzymes. Their charge-carrying ability is exactly what makes them 'electro'-lytes.
rationales.eli10: Electrolytes are like tiny batteries dissolved in your body's water. They carry little sparks of electricity that tell your nerves to send messages and your muscles to squeeze. They also help decide where water goes, keeping everything balanced.

questions.stem: Why does vitamin C consumed in the same meal improve the absorption of iron from plant foods?

options.text: It converts iron into heme iron, which is absorbed more easily
It blocks calcium so iron faces less competition
It reduces iron to a form that is more readily absorbed in the intestine
It raises stomach acid so iron can bind to fiber for uptake

rationales.whyCorrect: Non-heme iron from plants exists largely as ferric iron (Fe3+), which is poorly absorbed; vitamin C reduces it to the ferrous form (Fe2+) that the intestine takes up much more efficiently. This is why pairing beans or spinach with citrus or tomatoes boosts iron uptake. Vitamin C does not turn non-heme iron into heme iron, which is a separate form found in animal foods.
rationales.eli10: Plant iron comes in a 'locked' shape your gut has trouble grabbing. Vitamin C acts like a key that changes the iron into an 'unlocked' shape that slips right in. That is why a squeeze of lemon on your spinach helps you soak up more iron.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Non-heme iron from plants exists largely as ferric iron (Fe3+), which is poorly absorbed; vitamin C reduces it to the ferrous form (Fe2+) that the intestine takes up much more efficiently. This is why pairing beans or spinach with citrus or tomatoes boosts iron uptake. Vitamin C does not turn non-heme iron into heme iron, which is a separate form found in animal foods.

questions.stem: Which comparison between calcium and phosphorus is accurate?

options.text: Both are trace minerals needed in amounts under 100 mg per day
Phosphorus is stored in bone while calcium is found only in blood
Calcium is a mineral but phosphorus is a vitamin

questions.stem: What would most likely happen to the thyroid gland if a person's diet were severely deficient in iodine over a long period?

options.text: The gland would shrink and lower its hormone output
The gland would begin storing calcium instead of iodine
The gland would enlarge into a goiter as it tries to trap iodine
The gland would overproduce hormones and speed up metabolism

rationales.whyCorrect: Iodine is a required building block of thyroid hormones; when intake is too low, the pituitary releases more thyroid-stimulating hormone, causing the thyroid to enlarge into a goiter in an attempt to trap scarce iodine. This typically leads to hypothyroidism (a slowed metabolism), not overproduction. Iodized salt was introduced specifically to prevent this deficiency.
rationales.eli10: The thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones, like a bakery needs flour to make bread. If iodine runs low, the thyroid works overtime and swells up trying to grab every bit it can, creating a lump in the neck called a goiter. That is why table salt has iodine added.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Iodine is a required building block of thyroid hormones; when intake is too low, the pituitary releases more thyroid-stimulating hormone, causing the thyroid to enlarge into a goiter in an attempt to trap scarce iodine. questions.stem: A young woman who follows a vegetarian diet reports fatigue, pale skin, and shortness of breath during exercise. A deficiency of which mineral would best explain these findings?

rationales.whyCorrect: Iron is needed to make hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells; deficiency causes iron-deficiency anemia with fatigue, pallor, and breathlessness on exertion. Sodium, fluoride, and calcium deficiencies do not produce this classic anemia picture.
rationales.eli10: Iron helps your blood carry oxygen, like delivery trucks carrying air to every part of your body. Without enough iron, there are too few trucks, so you feel tired, look pale, and get out of breath easily. Plant foods have iron that is harder to absorb, so vegetarians have to be extra careful.

questions.stem: Which change to a person's eating pattern would most likely help lower elevated blood pressure, according to dietary guidance?

options.text: Increasing sodium and decreasing potassium intake
Eliminating calcium and magnesium from the diet
Decreasing sodium and increasing potassium-rich foods
Replacing water with sports drinks throughout the day

rationales.whyCorrect: High sodium intake pulls water into the bloodstream and raises blood volume and pressure, while potassium helps the body excrete sodium and relaxes blood vessel walls. Dietary approaches such as the DASH pattern therefore emphasize less sodium and more potassium-rich fruits and vegetables. Eliminating calcium and magnesium or substituting sugary sports drinks would not help and could be harmful.
rationales.eli10: Too much sodium is like adding extra water to a garden hose, making the pressure inside push harder. Potassium works the opposite way, helping flush out extra sodium and letting the 'hose' relax. So eating less salty food and more fruits and veggies eases the pressure.

Dietary approaches such as the DASH pattern therefore emphasize less sodium and more potassium-rich fruits and vegetables. questions.stem: An athlete drinks only plain water after several hours of heavy sweating and develops muscle cramps, nausea, and confusion. Which example best illustrates the underlying problem?

options.text: Excess calcium pulled from bone and building up in the muscles
Blood sodium diluted by replacing sweat loss with water alone
Too much iron released from red cells flooding the bloodstream
A sharp rise in blood potassium caused by drinking plain water

rationales.whyCorrect: Heavy sweating loses both water and sodium; replacing only water dilutes the remaining blood sodium, producing hyponatremia with cramps, nausea, and confusion. This is why endurance athletes are advised to replace electrolytes, not just fluid, during prolonged exertion. The scenario reflects too little sodium relative to water: sweating does not shift calcium from bone into muscle or release iron from red blood cells, and drinking plain water dilutes blood potassium rather than raising it.
rationales.eli10: Sweat carries out both water and salt. If you only pour plain water back in, the salt left in your blood gets watered down too much, like weak soup. When blood salt drops too low, muscles cramp and the brain gets foggy, so athletes need drinks with electrolytes, not just water.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Heavy sweating loses both water and sodium; replacing only water dilutes the remaining blood sodium, producing hyponatremia with cramps, nausea, and confusion. This is why endurance athletes are advised to replace electrolytes, not just fluid, during prolonged exertion. The scenario reflects too little sodium relative to water: sweating does not shift calcium from bone into muscle or release iron from red blood cells, and drinking plain water dilutes blood potassium rather than raising it.
