questions.stem: A person eats plenty of calcium-rich foods but has a diet very low in vitamin D. Which outcome is most likely, and why?

options.text: Calcium absorption stays normal because vitamin D acts only on the kidneys
Calcium absorption in the intestine falls because vitamin D drives uptake
Calcium is absorbed too quickly, driving blood calcium to dangerous levels
Calcium is converted into phosphorus to compensate for the missing vitamin

rationales.whyCorrect: Vitamin D promotes the synthesis of intestinal proteins that actively absorb dietary calcium, so a deficiency limits how much calcium the body can take up even when intake is adequate. Over time, poor calcium absorption can lead to inadequate bone mineralization despite a calcium-rich diet. Vitamin D acts on the intestine as well as the kidney and bone, minerals cannot be converted into other elements, and low vitamin D leads to less, not more, absorption.
rationales.eli10: Eating calcium is only step one; your body still needs a doorman to let it into the blood, and that doorman is vitamin D. Without vitamin D, most of the calcium you eat walks right past the door and leaves your body. So the two must work as a team for strong bones.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Vitamin D promotes the synthesis of intestinal proteins that actively absorb dietary calcium, so a deficiency limits how much calcium the body can take up even when intake is adequate. Over time, poor calcium absorption can lead to inadequate bone mineralization despite a calcium-rich diet. Vitamin D acts on the intestine as well as the kidney and bone, minerals cannot be converted into other elements, and low vitamin D leads to less, not more, absorption.

questions.stem: Two minerals often compete during intestinal absorption. Based on this principle, which situation is most likely to reduce zinc absorption?

options.text: Taking a high-dose iron supplement at the same time as zinc
Eating zinc-rich foods with a source of vitamin C
Consuming zinc with a small amount of dietary protein
Spreading zinc-containing foods across several meals

rationales.whyCorrect: Iron and zinc share absorption pathways in the intestine, so a large dose of one can competitively inhibit uptake of the other, which is why high-dose iron taken with zinc can lower zinc absorption. Vitamin C is not a meaningful inhibitor of zinc absorption (its well-known enhancing effect is on non-heme iron, not zinc), modest dietary protein tends to improve zinc absorption, and spreading intake across meals reduces competition. This mineral-mineral interaction is a key reason supplements are often timed apart.
rationales.eli10: Iron and zinc use the same narrow doorway to get into your blood. If a big crowd of iron shows up at once, it blocks the door so zinc can barely squeeze through. That is why taking large iron pills at the same time as zinc means you absorb less zinc.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Iron and zinc share absorption pathways in the intestine, so a large dose of one can competitively inhibit uptake of the other, which is why high-dose iron taken with zinc can lower zinc absorption. questions.stem: Which term best describes the mechanical and chemical breakdown of food into smaller molecules the body can absorb?

rationales.whyCorrect: Digestion is the process of breaking food down both mechanically (chewing, churning) and chemically (enzymes) into small molecules such as monosaccharides, amino acids, and fatty acids. Absorption is the later step in which those molecules cross the intestinal lining into the blood or lymph. Distinguishing these two processes is foundational to understanding how nutrients reach body cells.
rationales.eli10: Think of your food like a big LEGO castle. Digestion is taking the castle apart into single LEGO bricks so they are small enough to fit through a tiny door. That taking-apart step, using both your teeth and special juices, is digestion. Later, carrying the loose bricks through the door into your body is a different step called absorption.

questions.stem: Which organ is the primary site where most nutrient absorption takes place?

rationales.whyCorrect: The small intestine is where the majority of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals are absorbed, thanks to its enormous surface area created by folds, villi, and microvilli. The stomach mainly mixes and begins protein digestion, while the large intestine chiefly absorbs water and electrolytes. Recognizing the small intestine as the main absorptive organ explains why disorders affecting it cause widespread nutrient deficiencies.
rationales.eli10: The small intestine is like a super-long carpet folded up inside you, and the carpet is covered in tiny fuzzy fingers. All that fuzz gives a huge amount of surface to grab nutrients, kind of like how a towel soaks up more water than a flat plastic sheet. That is why almost all the good stuff from your food gets picked up there.

The stomach mainly mixes and begins protein digestion, while the large intestine chiefly absorbs water and electrolytes. questions.stem: Which statement correctly identifies the main role of bile in digestion?

options.text: It breaks the peptide bonds in proteins
It emulsifies fats into smaller droplets
It is the main source of the bicarbonate that neutralizes stomach acid entering the small intestine
It absorbs glucose directly into the bloodstream

rationales.whyCorrect: Bile is made by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and released into the duodenum, where it emulsifies large fat globules into many small droplets and greatly increases the surface area on which pancreatic lipase can act. This surfactant action is what makes efficient fat digestion and absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) possible. Bile is not an enzyme, so it cannot break the peptide bonds in proteins (A), and it does not carry glucose across the intestinal lining (D). Option C is a tempting near-miss: bile is an alkaline, bicarbonate-containing fluid and does help buffer acidic chyme, but the pancreas, not the liver, supplies the bulk of the bicarbonate that neutralizes chyme in the duodenum, so bile is not the main source. Emulsification is the role that belongs uniquely to bile.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a big blob of oil floating in water. It is hard to clean because it clumps together. Dish soap breaks that blob into lots of tiny droplets so it is easier to wash away. Bile works like that soap for the fat in your food, breaking one big fat blob into many little ones so the fat-digesting helpers can reach all of it. Bile is also a little bit like baking soda and helps calm the sour stomach juice, but the pancreas pours in most of that calming liquid. Soap for fat is bile's real specialty.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Bile is made by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and released into the duodenum, where it emulsifies large fat globules into many small droplets and greatly increases the surface area on which pancreatic lipase can act. This surfactant action is what makes efficient fat digestion and absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) possible. Bile is not an enzyme, so it cannot break the peptide bonds in proteins (A), and it does not carry glucose across the intestinal lining (D). Option C is a tempting near-miss: bile is an alkaline, bicarbonate-containing fluid and does help buffer acidic chyme, but the pancreas, not the liver, supplies the bulk of the bicarbonate that neutralizes chyme in the duodenum, so bile is not the main source. Emulsification is the role that belongs uniquely to bile.

questions.stem: Why does the small intestine have villi and microvilli covering its inner lining?

options.text: To store bile until fat arrives
To produce stomach acid more quickly
To slow food down so it can be chewed again
To increase surface area for absorption

rationales.whyCorrect: Villi are finger-like projections and microvilli are even smaller extensions on each cell, and together they multiply the intestinal surface area hundreds of times. This vastly expanded area allows far more nutrient molecules to be absorbed per unit of time. Without these structures, absorption would be too slow to meet the body's needs, which is why diseases that flatten villi (like celiac disease) cause malabsorption.
rationales.eli10: If you wanted to soak up spilled juice fast, a scrunched-up crinkly towel grabs way more than a flat one because it has more surface touching the juice. Villi and microvilli are all those crinkles and fuzz in your gut, giving a giant amount of surface so nutrients get soaked up quickly.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Villi are finger-like projections and microvilli are even smaller extensions on each cell, and together they multiply the intestinal surface area hundreds of times. This vastly expanded area allows far more nutrient molecules to be absorbed per unit of time. Without these structures, absorption would be too slow to meet the body's needs, which is why diseases that flatten villi (like celiac disease) cause malabsorption.

questions.stem: Which comparison between mechanical and chemical digestion is accurate?

options.text: Mechanical digestion breaks chemical bonds, while chemical digestion only moves food along
Both processes occur only in the stomach and nowhere else
Mechanical digestion physically breaks food apart, while chemical digestion uses enzymes to break bonds
Chemical digestion happens first and mechanical digestion happens only after absorption

rationales.whyCorrect: Mechanical digestion, such as chewing and stomach churning, physically reduces food size without changing its chemical structure, whereas chemical digestion uses enzymes to break covalent bonds and change food into absorbable molecules. Both begin in the mouth and continue in the stomach and small intestine, working together. Mechanical action increases surface area so enzymes in chemical digestion can act more effectively.
rationales.eli10: Mechanical digestion is like smashing a cracker into crumbs with your hands. The crumbs are smaller, but they are still cracker. Chemical digestion is like a magic juice that actually turns the cracker crumbs into something totally new and tiny. Smashing first just makes it easier for the magic juice to reach every bit.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the acidic environment created by the stomach?

options.text: To absorb most of the body's water
To emulsify dietary fats before they reach the liver
To activate the enzyme pepsin and begin protein digestion
To finish breaking down all carbohydrates into glucose

rationales.whyCorrect: Hydrochloric acid lowers stomach pH, which converts inactive pepsinogen into active pepsin so protein digestion can begin, and it also denatures proteins and kills many ingested microbes. Understanding this helps explain why the stomach focuses on protein while carbohydrate digestion, begun in the mouth, largely pauses in the acidic stomach.
rationales.eli10: Some tools only switch on in the right conditions, like a glow stick that only lights up after you snap it. The stomach's acid is the 'snap' that turns on the protein-cutting tool called pepsin. The sour acid also acts like a guard, zapping germs that sneak in with your food.

questions.stem: A person has surgery that removes a large portion of their small intestine. Based on its function, which outcome is most likely?

options.text: Increased absorption of all nutrients and vitamins
Impaired absorption of amino acids and glucose

rationales.eli10: The small intestine is your body's grabbing zone for nutrients. If you cut out a big chunk of the grabbing zone, there is less carpet and fuzz to catch the good stuff, so a lot of it slips past unabsorbed. Less grabbing area means less nutrition getting into the body.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates chemical digestion beginning in the mouth?

options.text: Teeth grinding a piece of bread into smaller pieces
Saliva moistening food so it slides down easily
The tongue pushing food toward the throat
Salivary amylase breaking starch into smaller sugars while chewing

rationales.whyCorrect: Salivary amylase is an enzyme in saliva that begins breaking the chemical bonds in starch, converting it into smaller carbohydrate units even before food is swallowed. Grinding by teeth, tongue movement, and moistening are mechanical or lubricating actions, not chemical bond breaking. This is why a starchy food like a cracker can start tasting slightly sweet the longer you chew it.
rationales.eli10: Ever notice a plain cracker starts tasting a little sweet if you chew it for a long time? That is because spit has a helper called amylase that snips the tasteless starch into small sweet sugars. That snipping of bonds is real chemical digestion, and it starts right in your mouth.

questions.stem: The large intestine reabsorbs water from undigested material. What would most likely happen if material moves through it too quickly?

rationales.whyCorrect: A major job of the large intestine is reabsorbing water and electrolytes, which normally firms the stool. If contents pass through too fast, there is less time for water reabsorption, so stools remain loose and watery, as in diarrhea. This cause-and-effect links the organ's function to a common real-world observation.
rationales.eli10: The large intestine is like a sponge that soaks water back out of leftover food so what leaves your body is firm. If the leftovers race through too fast, the sponge does not get enough time to soak up the water, so what comes out is runny and wet. That is what diarrhea is.

questions.stem: Absorbed amino acids and glucose travel a different route than most absorbed long-chain fats. Which comparison of these routes is accurate?

options.text: Amino acids and glucose enter lymphatic vessels, while long-chain fats enter blood capillaries to the liver
Both amino acids and long-chain fats enter lacteals in the villi and bypass the bloodstream entirely
Both amino acids and long-chain fats enter blood capillaries in the villi and bypass the liver completely
Amino acids and glucose travel via blood capillaries to the liver, while long-chain fats enter lymph first

rationales.whyCorrect: Water-soluble nutrients such as amino acids and glucose are absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi and travel via the hepatic portal vein to the liver for processing. Long-chain fatty acids are repackaged into chylomicrons that first enter lymphatic vessels (lacteals) and eventually join the bloodstream, bypassing the initial trip to the liver. Amino acids never enter the lacteals, and water-soluble nutrients absorbed into villus capillaries are delivered to the liver rather than bypassing it, so any option pairing the two nutrient classes on the same route is incorrect. Recognizing these two routes explains why fats and water-soluble nutrients are handled so differently after absorption.
rationales.eli10: After nutrients get grabbed, they take one of two roads home. Sugars and amino acids take the fast blood highway straight to the liver, the body's inspection station. Big fats are too greasy for that road, so they ride a separate milky path called the lymph first, then hop onto the blood later. Two nutrients, two different roads.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Water-soluble nutrients such as amino acids and glucose are absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi and travel via the hepatic portal vein to the liver for processing. Long-chain fatty acids are repackaged into chylomicrons that first enter lymphatic vessels (lacteals) and eventually join the bloodstream, bypassing the initial trip to the liver. questions.stem: What would happen if the pancreas failed to release its digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the small intestine?

options.text: Carbohydrate, protein, and fat digestion would be impaired and intestinal contents would remain too acidic
Digestion would improve because fewer enzymes reduce the digestive workload
Only water absorption in the large intestine would be affected, sparing the macronutrients
The stomach would stop producing acid to compensate for the missing secretions

rationales.whyCorrect: The pancreas secretes enzymes (such as pancreatic amylase, proteases, and lipase) that digest all three macronutrients, plus bicarbonate that neutralizes acidic chyme arriving from the stomach. Without them, macronutrient digestion is severely impaired, and the unneutralized acid can damage the intestinal lining and inactivate remaining enzymes, which work best at a neutral pH. This integrates the pancreas's dual digestive roles into one outcome.
rationales.eli10: The pancreas does two big jobs at once: it sends in a whole toolkit of food-cutting helpers, and it pours in a baking-soda-like liquid to calm down the stomach acid. If it stops, the food does not get cut up properly and the gut stays too sour, which even breaks the few helpers that are left. So digestion of sugars, proteins, and fats all suffer.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The pancreas secretes enzymes (such as pancreatic amylase, proteases, and lipase) that digest all three macronutrients, plus bicarbonate that neutralizes acidic chyme arriving from the stomach. Without them, macronutrient digestion is severely impaired, and the unneutralized acid can damage the intestinal lining and inactivate remaining enzymes, which work best at a neutral pH. This integrates the pancreas's dual digestive roles into one outcome.

questions.stem: Which term best describes the total amount of energy the body uses in a day?

rationales.whyCorrect: Total daily energy expenditure (TDEE) is the sum of all energy the body uses in 24 hours, combining basal metabolic rate, the thermic effect of food, and physical activity. Basal metabolic rate and the thermic effect of food are only components of TDEE, not the whole, so they are narrower terms.
rationales.eli10: Think of your body like a phone that uses battery all day. TDEE is the total battery you drain from morning to night, added up from everything: the background apps always running (basal metabolism), digesting food, and moving around. The other terms are just single apps, not the full total.

Basal metabolic rate and the thermic effect of food are only components of TDEE, not the whole, so they are narrower terms.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines basal metabolic rate (BMR)?

options.text: The energy used to digest and absorb nutrients from a meal
The energy used at complete rest to maintain vital functions
The energy burned during moderate exercise and household chores
The daily calories eaten minus the calories stored as fat

rationales.whyCorrect: Basal metabolic rate is the energy required at complete rest to keep essential processes running, such as breathing, heartbeat, and cell activity. It excludes the energy used to digest and absorb nutrients (the thermic effect of food) and the energy used for exercise and daily chores (physical activity), which are measured separately, and it is not an intake-minus-storage calculation.
rationales.eli10: Even when you are lying totally still doing nothing, your heart beats, your lungs breathe, and your cells keep working. BMR is the fuel needed just to stay alive and 'idling,' like a car engine running while parked. It is the biggest chunk of energy most people use each day.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Basal metabolic rate is the energy required at complete rest to keep essential processes running, such as breathing, heartbeat, and cell activity. It excludes the energy used to digest and absorb nutrients (the thermic effect of food) and the energy used for exercise and daily chores (physical activity), which are measured separately, and it is not an intake-minus-storage calculation.

questions.stem: Energy balance is achieved when which of the following is true?

options.text: Energy intake is less than energy expenditure
Energy intake is greater than energy expenditure
Energy intake comes only from carbohydrates

rationales.whyCorrect: Energy balance describes a state where calories consumed equal calories used, so body weight remains stable over time. When intake exceeds expenditure the result is positive balance (weight gain), and when expenditure exceeds intake it is negative balance (weight loss).
rationales.eli10: Imagine a bank account where the money you put in matches the money you spend. Your balance stays the same. With energy, when the calories you eat match the calories you burn, your weight holds steady. That perfect match is called energy balance.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Energy balance describes a state where calories consumed equal calories used, so body weight remains stable over time. When intake exceeds expenditure the result is positive balance (weight gain), and when expenditure exceeds intake it is negative balance (weight loss).

questions.stem: Why does having more lean muscle mass tend to raise a person's basal metabolic rate?

options.text: Muscle tissue slows digestion, keeping food energy in the body longer
Muscle tissue stores more water, which requires calories to maintain
Muscle tissue is metabolically active and burns more energy at rest than fat tissue
Muscle tissue insulates the body, reducing the need for warmth

rationales.whyCorrect: Lean muscle is metabolically active tissue that consumes more energy even at rest compared with adipose (fat) tissue. Therefore, individuals with greater muscle mass generally have a higher BMR, which is one reason body composition, not just body weight, influences energy needs.
rationales.eli10: Muscle is like a hungry, always-on machine, while fat is more like a quiet storage box. Even when you sit still, muscle keeps asking for fuel to stay ready. So the more muscle you carry, the more calories you burn just resting.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Lean muscle is metabolically active tissue that consumes more energy even at rest compared with adipose (fat) tissue. Therefore, individuals with greater muscle mass generally have a higher BMR, which is one reason body composition, not just body weight, influences energy needs.

questions.stem: Which comparison between the thermic effect of food and physical activity is accurate?

options.text: Both contribute equally and together form the largest part of total daily energy use
The thermic effect of food is larger than basal metabolic rate in most healthy adults
Physical activity is fixed across individuals, while the thermic effect of food varies daily
The thermic effect of food is small and stable, while physical activity varies the most

rationales.whyCorrect: The thermic effect of food (energy used to digest, absorb, and process nutrients) accounts for roughly 10 percent of total energy expenditure and stays relatively stable. Physical activity is the component people can change the most, making it the most variable part of total daily energy expenditure. Basal metabolic rate, not the thermic effect of food, is the largest component, and it is activity rather than digestion that varies from person to person and day to day.
rationales.eli10: Digesting food usually takes about the same small slice of the calories you eat, roughly a tenth, so as a share of your day it does not swing much. (Protein costs a bit more to digest than carbs or fat.) But how much you move around, from lying on the couch to running errands all day, can change a lot day to day. That is why exercise is the part you can most easily change.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The thermic effect of food (energy used to digest, absorb, and process nutrients) accounts for roughly 10 percent of total energy expenditure and stays relatively stable. Physical activity is the component people can change the most, making it the most variable part of total daily energy expenditure. Basal metabolic rate, not the thermic effect of food, is the largest component, and it is activity rather than digestion that varies from person to person and day to day.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen to body weight over time if a person consistently consumes more energy than they expend?

options.text: Body weight would decrease due to negative energy balance
Body weight would increase as excess energy is stored, largely as fat
Body weight would stay the same due to energy balance
Body weight would decrease as the body burns stored protein

rationales.whyCorrect: Consistently eating more calories than are used creates a positive energy balance. The surplus energy is stored in the body, primarily as adipose (fat) tissue, leading to weight gain over time.
rationales.eli10: If you keep putting more into a backpack than you take out, it gets heavier. When you eat more energy than you use, your body tucks the extra away, mostly as fat, so your weight slowly climbs. That extra-in situation is called positive energy balance.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Consistently eating more calories than are used creates a positive energy balance. The surplus energy is stored in the body, primarily as adipose (fat) tissue, leading to weight gain over time.

questions.stem: A pre-nursing student notices that two adults of the same weight have different calorie needs. Which factor best explains this difference?

options.text: One ate a larger breakfast on the morning they were compared
Both are the same height and have the same body mass index
One drinks more water with meals than the other does each day
One has more lean muscle mass and is more physically active

rationales.whyCorrect: Even at identical body weights, differences in body composition (muscle versus fat) and physical activity level change energy needs. More muscle raises BMR and more activity raises the activity component, so the more muscular, active person needs more calories. A single larger meal, matching height or BMI, and water intake do not meaningfully change how many calories a person needs.

rationales.distractorAnalysis: Even at identical body weights, differences in body composition (muscle versus fat) and physical activity level change energy needs. questions.stem: Which example best illustrates a person in negative energy balance?

options.text: An athlete who eats extra food to gain muscle and gains weight
A person who increases exercise and reduces intake and gradually loses weight
An adult whose weight has been stable for a year on a steady diet
A person who eats a large dessert after a normal-sized dinner

rationales.whyCorrect: Negative energy balance occurs when energy expenditure exceeds intake, leading to weight loss as the body draws on stored energy. Increasing exercise while eating less creates that deficit, which is why gradual weight loss follows.
rationales.eli10: If you spend more money than you earn, your savings shrink. Burning more calories than you eat makes your body dip into its stored fuel, so weight goes down. Exercising more and eating a bit less is the classic recipe for that 'spending more than you earn' state.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Negative energy balance occurs when energy expenditure exceeds intake, leading to weight loss as the body draws on stored energy. Increasing exercise while eating less creates that deficit, which is why gradual weight loss follows.

questions.stem: A patient's chart notes that most of their daily calorie burn comes from staying alive at rest. Which component of energy expenditure does this describe, and why is it usually the largest?

options.text: Thermic effect of food, because digestion runs constantly
Physical activity, because everyone moves throughout the day
Basal metabolic rate, because vital organ functions run continuously
Adaptive thermogenesis, because the body always adjusts to cold

rationales.whyCorrect: Basal metabolic rate typically accounts for the largest share (often 60 to 70 percent) of total daily energy expenditure because organs like the brain, heart, liver, and kidneys use energy around the clock. Digestion and activity add to this but usually contribute less.
rationales.eli10: Your body's 'always-on' systems, like your brain thinking and heart beating, never take a break, so they quietly use most of your energy every day. That baseline is your basal metabolic rate, and because it runs 24/7, it is usually the biggest slice of the energy pie.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Basal metabolic rate typically accounts for the largest share (often 60 to 70 percent) of total daily energy expenditure because organs like the brain, heart, liver, and kidneys use energy around the clock. questions.stem: During prolonged calorie restriction, some people find weight loss slows even though they keep eating less. Which concept best explains this plateau?

options.text: Adaptive thermogenesis lowers energy expenditure as the body conserves energy
The thermic effect of food rises sharply to burn the stored fat
Basal metabolic rate rises to match the reduced intake
Physical activity automatically increases to restore energy balance

rationales.whyCorrect: With prolonged energy restriction and weight loss, the body reduces its energy expenditure through adaptive thermogenesis and a lower BMR (partly from lost tissue). This narrows the energy deficit, slowing further weight loss even when intake stays low.
rationales.eli10: When food gets scarce for a long time, your body acts like a phone switching to low-power mode to save battery. It burns fuel more slowly to hang on to what it has. That energy-saving slowdown is called adaptive thermogenesis, and it makes losing more weight harder.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: With prolonged energy restriction and weight loss, the body reduces its energy expenditure through adaptive thermogenesis and a lower BMR (partly from lost tissue). This narrows the energy deficit, slowing further weight loss even when intake stays low.

questions.stem: Which comparison of positive and negative energy balance is accurate regarding how the body handles the energy mismatch?

options.text: In positive balance the body stores surplus energy, while in negative balance it mobilizes stored energy
In positive balance the body burns stored fat, while in negative balance it stores fat
Both states cause the body to store energy, differing only in speed
Both states keep body weight stable because metabolism always compensates fully

rationales.whyCorrect: Positive energy balance means intake exceeds expenditure, so the surplus is stored (mainly as fat), causing weight gain. Negative energy balance means expenditure exceeds intake, so the body draws on stored energy, causing weight loss. The two states move energy in opposite directions.
rationales.eli10: Think of a savings account. When you earn more than you spend (positive balance), money piles up in savings. When you spend more than you earn (negative balance), you pull from savings. Your body does the same with energy, storing the extra or dipping into its fat reserves.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Positive energy balance means intake exceeds expenditure, so the surplus is stored (mainly as fat), causing weight gain. Negative energy balance means expenditure exceeds intake, so the body draws on stored energy, causing weight loss. The two states move energy in opposite directions.

questions.stem: For most healthy infants, which of the following is recommended as the only food source during about the first 6 months of life?

options.text: Whole cow's milk fortified with vitamin D
Diluted 100% fruit juice given in a bottle
Iron-fortified rice cereal mixed with water

rationales.whyCorrect: Major authorities including the USDA/HHS Dietary Guidelines recommend exclusive breastfeeding, or iron-fortified formula when breast milk is unavailable, for about the first 6 months because it supplies complete, age-appropriate nutrition and immune protection (breastfed infants are also given a vitamin D supplement, which is a supplement rather than a food). Whole cow's milk is not recommended before 12 months, and juice and solids are introduced later. This establishes the baseline of infant feeding.
rationales.eli10: A newborn's stomach and kidneys are still tiny and delicate, like a brand-new engine that can only run on one special fuel. Breast milk (or iron-fortified formula, the backup fuel) is made to match exactly what a baby can handle, though breastfed babies also usually get vitamin D drops. Cow's milk and juice are too heavy for that little engine at first, so they come later.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Major authorities including the USDA/HHS Dietary Guidelines recommend exclusive breastfeeding, or iron-fortified formula when breast milk is unavailable, for about the first 6 months because it supplies complete, age-appropriate nutrition and immune protection (breastfed infants are also given a vitamin D supplement, which is a supplement rather than a food). Whole cow's milk is not recommended before 12 months, and juice and solids are introduced later. This establishes the baseline of infant feeding.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines a 'nutrient-dense' food, a concept emphasized across all life stages?

options.text: A food that supplies many vitamins and minerals per calorie
A food that is high in saturated fat, added sugar, and sodium
A food that provides many calories relative to its weight
A food fortified with added sugar to supply quick energy

rationales.whyCorrect: The Dietary Guidelines define nutrient-dense foods as those delivering vitamins, minerals, and other beneficial substances with relatively few calories and little added sugar, saturated fat, or sodium. This contrasts with energy-dense but nutrient-poor foods. The concept guides healthy choices at every age.
rationales.eli10: Think of your daily calories as a small backpack with limited space. A nutrient-dense food is like a small item packed full of useful gear, lots of value for little space. A candy bar takes up the same space but is mostly filler. You want the most helpful stuff per pocket of space.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The Dietary Guidelines define nutrient-dense foods as those delivering vitamins, minerals, and other beneficial substances with relatively few calories and little added sugar, saturated fat, or sodium. questions.stem: Which nutrient is recommended in increased amounts before and during early pregnancy specifically to reduce the risk of neural tube defects?

rationales.whyCorrect: Folate, and its synthetic form folic acid, is essential for DNA synthesis and proper closure of the neural tube in early embryonic development. Health authorities recommend women capable of pregnancy consume adequate folic acid, because the neural tube closes before many women know they are pregnant. Deficiency is linked to defects such as spina bifida.
rationales.eli10: In the first weeks, a baby's spinal cord zips itself closed like a jacket. Folate is the helper that makes sure the zipper goes all the way up without gaps. Because this zipping happens super early, moms need plenty of folate even before they know a baby is on the way.

Health authorities recommend women capable of pregnancy consume adequate folic acid, because the neural tube closes before many women know they are pregnant. Deficiency is linked to defects such as spina bifida.

questions.stem: What is the primary reason infants have a much higher fluid and calorie requirement per pound of body weight than adults?

options.text: Infants have fully mature kidneys that excrete water wastefully
Infants store more body fat, which raises their resting energy burn
Infants grow rapidly and have a high metabolic rate for their size
Infants are much less physically active than adults throughout the day

rationales.whyCorrect: During infancy, the body builds new tissue at an extraordinary rate and has a high metabolic rate combined with a large surface-area-to-mass ratio, driving up needs for energy and fluids per unit of weight. rationales.eli10: A baby is like a house being built super fast, workers need tons of supplies delivered constantly. Grown-ups are like a finished house that just needs upkeep. Pound for pound, the busy construction site (the baby) needs way more fuel and water to keep building.

questions.stem: Which change in older adults would most likely increase their risk of dehydration compared with younger adults?

options.text: Blunted thirst signals and reduced kidney concentrating ability
Higher total body water reserves that buffer everyday fluid losses
Heightened thirst sensation that prompts frequent drinking
Faster gastric emptying that speeds absorption of oral fluids

rationales.whyCorrect: With aging, the thirst mechanism becomes blunted and the kidneys are less able to concentrate urine and conserve water, so older adults may not feel thirsty even when fluid-depleted. Total body water also declines with age, leaving less reserve. Together these changes raise dehydration risk.
rationales.eli10: Thirst is your body's alarm bell for 'drink water,' and the kidneys are the sponge that holds water in. As people get older, the alarm gets quieter and the sponge holds less. So an older person can be low on water without their body shouting about it.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: With aging, the thirst mechanism becomes blunted and the kidneys are less able to concentrate urine and conserve water, so older adults may not feel thirsty even when fluid-depleted. Total body water also declines with age, leaving less reserve. Together these changes raise dehydration risk.

questions.stem: Which comparison between adolescence and other life stages is accurate regarding nutrition?

options.text: Adolescents require less protein than infants per pound because tissue building is already complete
Adolescents need fewer calories than young children because growth has stopped
Adolescents have high needs for calcium and iron to support the growth spurt and, in females, menstruation
Adolescent nutrient needs are essentially identical to those of sedentary older adults

rationales.whyCorrect: The adolescent growth spurt dramatically raises needs for energy, calcium (for peak bone mass), and iron (for expanding blood volume and muscle, plus menstrual losses in females). These needs are among the highest of any life stage after infancy. Recognizing this explains common teen deficiencies like inadequate calcium and iron.
rationales.eli10: Teenagers grow fast, taller bones, more muscle, more blood. Calcium is the material for building strong bones, and iron helps make the extra blood. So teens are like a growth factory that suddenly needs big shipments of building materials again.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The adolescent growth spurt dramatically raises needs for energy, calcium (for peak bone mass), and iron (for expanding blood volume and muscle, plus menstrual losses in females). questions.stem: What would most likely happen if solid foods were introduced to an infant well before about 6 months of age?

options.text: It would guarantee earlier achievement of walking and talking milestones
It would improve iron absorption because the infant gut is fully mature
It would eliminate the need for breast milk or formula feedings entirely
It could raise choking risk and displace nutrient-rich milk feedings

rationales.whyCorrect: Very early introduction of solids is discouraged because young infants lack the neuromuscular readiness (head control, coordinated swallowing) and mature digestive function needed, raising choking risk and potentially displacing calorie- and nutrient-rich milk. rationales.eli10: A baby's mouth and tummy need practice and time before they can handle solid food, like you can't drive a car before your feet reach the pedals. Push food in too soon and the baby might choke or fill up on food that has less good stuff than milk. Waiting until they're ready keeps them safe and well-fed.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman asks why her recommended daily calorie intake barely changes in the first trimester but rises later. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: Calorie needs stay constant across all three trimesters because fetal growth is steady
Calorie needs rise late in pregnancy only because maternal physical activity increases
The largest calorie increase comes in the first trimester, when the embryo's organs form
Fetal and maternal tissue growth is greatest during the second and third trimesters

rationales.eli10: In early pregnancy the baby is tiny, like a seed, so it barely needs extra food. Later the baby grows fast into something much bigger, and mom's body adds more blood and tissue too. That's when the extra calories are really needed, so the increase comes later, not at the start.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Energy needs in pregnancy increase modestly and mainly in the second and third trimesters, when fetal growth, expanded blood volume, and maternal tissue (uterus, placenta, fat stores) grow most rapidly. questions.stem: Which example best illustrates addressing a common nutrition concern of the toddler years (ages 1-3)?

options.text: Switching entirely to skim milk and eliminating all dietary fat before age 2
Giving unlimited juice throughout the day to ensure adequate fluid and vitamin intake
Offering small portions of varied nutrient-dense foods repeatedly without pressure
Requiring the child to finish every plate at every meal to prevent nutrient deficiency

rationales.whyCorrect: Toddler growth slows compared with infancy, so appetite naturally decreases and becomes erratic, and food neophobia (wariness of new foods) is common. Repeated, pressure-free exposure to varied nutrient-dense foods supports acceptance and adequate intake. rationales.eli10: Little kids grow slower than babies, so they eat less and can be picky, refusing a food one day and liking it later. The trick is to keep calmly offering good foods in small amounts, like planting seeds again and again. Forcing them or filling them with juice backfires.

questions.stem: An older adult reports poor appetite, uses several medications, and lives alone. Which interpretation best explains why she is at elevated nutritional risk?

options.text: Higher calorie needs together with higher nutrient needs make balancing her daily intake straightforward
Lower calorie needs with unchanged or higher nutrient needs, compounded by medications and isolation
Medications reliably improve nutrient absorption, offsetting any dietary shortfalls in older adults
Living alone tends to increase appetite, so the main risk is overnutrition rather than deficiency

rationales.whyCorrect: Aging typically lowers energy needs (less muscle mass, lower activity) while needs for several nutrients stay the same or rise, so every calorie must be more nutrient-dense. Polypharmacy can affect appetite and absorption, and social isolation reduces meal quality, compounding risk. This combination is a classic reason older adults are vulnerable to undernutrition.
rationales.eli10: Older bodies burn fewer calories but still need lots of vitamins, so there's less room to fit in all the good stuff, every bite has to count. Add pills that dull appetite and eating alone with no one to cook for, and it gets easy to miss out on nutrients. Several small problems stack into one big risk.

questions.stem: A lactating mother wonders how her nutritional needs during breastfeeding compare with her needs during pregnancy. Which comparison is accurate?

options.text: Lactation raises energy and fluid needs, often above pregnancy levels, to sustain milk production
Lactation requires no additional calories because milk is made entirely from fat stored in pregnancy
Nutrient needs during lactation drop back to pre-pregnancy levels immediately after delivery
Breastfeeding requires fewer total daily calories than the non-pregnant, non-lactating state

rationales.whyCorrect: Producing milk is energetically costly, with a total energy cost of roughly 500 kcal/day; part is met by fat stored during pregnancy, but additional dietary intake is still required, and estimated added needs are on the order of, and often exceed, those of pregnancy. Fluid needs also rise to support milk volume. This explains why lactating women are advised to eat and drink more than usual.
rationales.eli10: Making milk every day is hard work, like running a small factory that never closes. That factory needs extra fuel and lots of water to keep the milk flowing, as much as or more than growing the baby did. Some energy comes from fat saved up during pregnancy, but mom still needs to eat and drink extra.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Producing milk is energetically costly, with a total energy cost of roughly 500 kcal/day; part is met by fat stored during pregnancy, but additional dietary intake is still required, and estimated added needs are on the order of, and often exceed, those of pregnancy. questions.stem: Which statement best integrates the concept of 'peak bone mass' across the lifespan?

options.text: Bone density is set at birth and cannot be meaningfully changed by diet at any later life stage
Calcium and vitamin D in childhood and adolescence build peak bone mass, lowering osteoporosis risk
Peak bone mass is not reached until older adulthood, so calcium and vitamin D matter most after age 65
Only weight-bearing exercise, not dietary calcium or vitamin D, determines lifelong bone strength

rationales.whyCorrect: Bone is built most rapidly during childhood and adolescence, with peak bone mass generally reached by the late teens to twenties; adequate calcium and vitamin D during these years help maximize that peak. A higher peak provides a larger reserve against the gradual bone loss of aging, lowering later osteoporosis risk. This connects early-life nutrition to late-life health, though exercise also contributes.
rationales.eli10: Think of bone as a savings account you fill up most when you're young. The more calcium and vitamin D you 'deposit' as a kid and teen, the bigger your bone bank gets. Later in life everyone slowly withdraws bone, so starting with a fuller account keeps bones stronger for longer.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Bone is built most rapidly during childhood and adolescence, with peak bone mass generally reached by the late teens to twenties; adequate calcium and vitamin D during these years help maximize that peak. A higher peak provides a larger reserve against the gradual bone loss of aging, lowering later osteoporosis risk. questions.stem: Which term describes a long-lasting health condition, such as type 2 diabetes or heart disease, that generally progresses slowly and is strongly influenced by diet and lifestyle?

rationales.whyCorrect: A chronic disease is a condition lasting a year or more that typically progresses gradually and often requires ongoing management; many chronic diseases (heart disease, type 2 diabetes, some cancers) share diet-related risk factors. This contrasts with acute illnesses, which come on quickly and resolve, and with infectious diseases caused by pathogens. Recognizing this category matters because nutrition is a major modifiable factor in preventing and managing chronic disease.
rationales.eli10: Think of a chronic disease as a houseguest who moves in and stays for years, not a cold that visits for a weekend. Because it sticks around, the everyday choices you make, especially what you eat, really shape how it behaves over time. That slow, long-term nature is exactly what the word chronic means.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly identifies a dietary factor most strongly linked to raising blood pressure in salt-sensitive individuals?

rationales.whyCorrect: Excess dietary sodium causes the body to retain water to keep sodium concentration balanced, increasing blood volume and thus blood pressure, especially in salt-sensitive people. The Dietary Guidelines recommend limiting sodium to help prevent and manage hypertension. Potassium and fiber generally have the opposite, blood-pressure-lowering effect.
rationales.eli10: Salt acts like a sponge in your blood, pulling in extra water. More water in the pipes means more pressure pushing on the walls, just like a garden hose swells when you crank the tap. That is why cutting back on sodium helps keep blood pressure down.

questions.stem: Which nutrient-related change is a core recommendation for lowering LDL ("bad") cholesterol and reducing heart disease risk?

options.text: Increasing intake of processed red meats
Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats

rationales.whyCorrect: Swapping saturated fats (found in fatty meats, butter) for unsaturated fats (found in olive oil, nuts, fish) lowers LDL cholesterol and is recommended by the Dietary Guidelines for cardiovascular health. Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL and should be avoided, and eliminating all fat is neither necessary nor healthy because the body needs essential fatty acids. This substitution is more effective than simply cutting total fat.
rationales.eli10: Not all fats behave the same way. Saturated and trans fats push up the amount of "bad" LDL cholesterol floating in your blood, and it is that extra LDL working its way into artery walls that slowly builds plaque. Unsaturated fats from things like fish, nuts, and olive oil nudge that number down instead, so trading them in helps keep your blood highways clearer.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Swapping saturated fats (found in fatty meats, butter) for unsaturated fats (found in olive oil, nuts, fish) lowers LDL cholesterol and is recommended by the Dietary Guidelines for cardiovascular health. Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL and should be avoided, and eliminating all fat is neither necessary nor healthy because the body needs essential fatty acids. questions.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which soluble fiber helps improve blood cholesterol levels?

options.text: It is absorbed into the bloodstream, where it dissolves LDL cholesterol directly
It binds bile acids for excretion, so the liver uses cholesterol to make more
It blocks the pancreas from releasing the lipase enzymes that digest dietary fat
It converts LDL cholesterol into HDL cholesterol inside the intestinal wall lining

rationales.whyCorrect: Soluble fiber forms a gel that binds bile acids (which are made from cholesterol) and carries them out in the stool; the liver then pulls cholesterol from the blood to synthesize new bile acids, lowering circulating LDL. Fiber is not absorbed into the blood, it does not block pancreatic lipase secretion, and it cannot chemically convert one lipoprotein into another. This mechanism explains why oats, beans, and barley are recommended for heart health.
rationales.eli10: Bile is a digestive juice your body builds out of cholesterol. Soluble fiber grabs that bile like a sticky net and drags it out of your body. To make more bile, your liver has to pull cholesterol out of your blood, so your cholesterol level drops.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Soluble fiber forms a gel that binds bile acids (which are made from cholesterol) and carries them out in the stool; the liver then pulls cholesterol from the blood to synthesize new bile acids, lowering circulating LDL. Fiber is not absorbed into the blood, it does not block pancreatic lipase secretion, and it cannot chemically convert one lipoprotein into another. This mechanism explains why oats, beans, and barley are recommended for heart health.

questions.stem: Which comparison between type 1 and type 2 diabetes is accurate?

options.text: Type 1 is primarily prevented by diet, while type 2 is an autoimmune attack on the pancreas
Both types are caused by the pancreas releasing too much insulin in response to meals
Type 1 involves little or no insulin production, while type 2 involves insulin resistance
Type 2 always requires insulin injections from diagnosis, while type 1 is managed by diet

rationales.whyCorrect: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the pancreas produces little or no insulin, so it is not prevented by diet. Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance (cells respond poorly to insulin) and is strongly associated with modifiable factors like weight and diet, and many people manage it initially without insulin injections. Both types result in elevated blood glucose but through different mechanisms.
rationales.eli10: Insulin is the key that lets sugar into your cells. In type 1, the body can't make the key at all. In type 2, the body makes keys but the locks get rusty and stop working well, and that rustiness is often tied to weight and eating habits.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the pancreas produces little or no insulin, so it is not prevented by diet. Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance (cells respond poorly to insulin) and is strongly associated with modifiable factors like weight and diet, and many people manage it initially without insulin injections. Both types result in elevated blood glucose but through different mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which change would most likely reduce the risk of large blood-glucose spikes after a meal for someone managing type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Choosing refined white bread over whole grains
Eating carbohydrates alone on an empty stomach
Pairing carbohydrates with fiber, protein, or healthy fat

rationales.whyCorrect: Fiber, protein, and fat slow gastric emptying and carbohydrate digestion, producing a more gradual rise in blood glucose rather than a sharp spike. Refined grains and sugary drinks are digested quickly and cause rapid glucose surges. Combining foods is a practical strategy that lowers the effective glycemic response of a meal.
rationales.eli10: Sugar by itself races into your blood like water down a slide. Fiber, protein, and fat act like speed bumps that slow the sugar down, so it trickles in instead of flooding in. A steadier flow is much easier for the body to handle.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the DASH eating pattern?

options.text: To promote rapid weight loss by eliminating all dietary carbohydrate and fat
To treat celiac disease by removing every gluten-containing grain from meals
To increase protein intake for building muscle mass in strength-training athletes
To lower blood pressure with produce and low-fat dairy while limiting sodium

rationales.whyCorrect: DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) was designed specifically to reduce blood pressure; it is rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium, and fiber from produce, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while limiting sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars. It is not a low-carb, gluten-free, or high-protein athletic plan. Research shows it lowers blood pressure and supports overall cardiovascular health.
rationales.eli10: DASH is like a recipe for calmer blood pressure. It loads your plate with fruits, veggies, whole grains, and low-fat dairy, which are full of minerals that relax blood vessels, and it dials back the salt that raises pressure. The whole point is a gentler push on your artery walls.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) was designed specifically to reduce blood pressure; it is rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium, and fiber from produce, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while limiting sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars. questions.stem: A person reads a food label showing a product high in added sugars and refined grains but low in fiber. Which chronic-disease concern is this pattern most directly associated with when eaten regularly?

options.text: Increased risk of iron-deficiency anemia only

Over time that pattern wears out the body's sugar-handling system, which is how type 2 diabetes and weight gain creep in.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates a heart-healthy substitution consistent with reducing cardiovascular disease risk?

options.text: Replacing grilled salmon with fried chicken
Replacing white rice with brown rice at dinner
Replacing a handful of walnuts with potato chips
Replacing olive oil with butter for cooking

rationales.whyCorrect: Choosing brown rice (a whole grain) over white rice (refined) adds fiber and nutrients and supports better blood glucose and cholesterol control, consistent with cardiovascular disease prevention. The other options move from healthier choices (fish, olive oil, nuts) toward foods higher in saturated or trans fats and refined starches. Whole-grain substitutions are a hallmark of heart-healthy eating patterns.
rationales.eli10: Brown rice keeps its outer coat, which is full of fiber, while white rice has that coat polished off. Keeping the coat means more fiber to slow digestion and help your heart. The other swaps go the wrong way, trading good foods for greasier or emptier ones.

questions.stem: A dietary plan emphasizes potassium-rich foods like bananas, leafy greens, and beans for someone with high blood pressure. What is the primary reason potassium is beneficial here?

options.text: Potassium helps the body excrete sodium and relax blood vessel walls
Potassium adds bulk to the stool, easing constipation and bloating
Potassium expands total blood volume, which raises cardiac output
Potassium binds dietary cholesterol in the intestine so it is excreted

rationales.whyCorrect: Potassium helps the body excrete sodium and relaxes blood vessel walls, both of which lower blood pressure; this is a key reason the DASH pattern emphasizes potassium-rich produce. It does not expand blood volume, and its cardiovascular benefit is unrelated to stool bulk or cholesterol binding. Most Americans consume too little potassium, making it a nutrient of public health concern.
rationales.eli10: If sodium is the bully that raises your blood pressure, potassium is the helper that shows sodium the door and tells your blood vessels to relax. Both actions take pressure off your artery walls, which is why potassium-rich foods are so useful for high blood pressure.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Potassium helps the body excrete sodium and relaxes blood vessel walls, both of which lower blood pressure; this is a key reason the DASH pattern emphasizes potassium-rich produce. It does not expand blood volume, and its cardiovascular benefit is unrelated to stool bulk or cholesterol binding. Most Americans consume too little potassium, making it a nutrient of public health concern.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen to overall chronic-disease risk if a person consistently followed an eating pattern high in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and fish while limiting processed meats, added sugars, and refined grains?

options.text: Risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers would tend to decrease
Risk would rise sharply due to excessive fiber intake
Risk of type 1 diabetes would be eliminated
Chronic-disease risk would be unchanged because diet has little long-term effect

rationales.whyCorrect: This describes a pattern similar to the Mediterranean and DASH styles that the Dietary Guidelines associate with lower risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers because it is rich in fiber, unsaturated fats, and protective phytochemicals while low in components that drive disease. Diet strongly influences these outcomes, but type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and not preventable by diet. Fiber at these levels is beneficial, not harmful.
rationales.eli10: Eating mostly plants, whole grains, and fish while going easy on processed meat and sugar is like giving your body high-quality fuel year after year. That steady care lowers the odds of several big diseases at once. But it can't stop type 1 diabetes, because that one comes from the immune system, not the plate.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: This describes a pattern similar to the Mediterranean and DASH styles that the Dietary Guidelines associate with lower risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers because it is rich in fiber, unsaturated fats, and protective phytochemicals while low in components that drive disease. Diet strongly influences these outcomes, but type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and not preventable by diet. Fiber at these levels is beneficial, not harmful.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a dietary strategy with the chronic disease it most directly helps prevent or manage?

options.text: Higher soluble fiber intake, which helps prevent autoimmune type 1 diabetes
Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake, which helps reduce the risk of osteoporosis
Lower dietary potassium intake, which helps lower chronically high blood pressure
Eliminating all dietary fat, which helps prevent coronary heart disease

rationales.whyCorrect: Adequate calcium supports bone mineral density and vitamin D promotes calcium absorption, so together they help prevent osteoporosis, a common diet-related chronic condition. The other pairings are backwards: soluble fiber benefits cholesterol and blood glucose but cannot prevent autoimmune type 1 diabetes; potassium should be increased, not reduced, to help lower blood pressure; and some unsaturated fat is essential, so eliminating all dietary fat is not a heart-disease prevention strategy.
rationales.eli10: Picture your bones as a vault of calcium, with vitamin D acting as the guard who unlocks the door so calcium can get inside. Keep both well stocked and the vault stays strong, which is how you fend off the brittle bones of osteoporosis. The other pairings flip the roles around, so they simply don't hold up.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Adequate calcium supports bone mineral density and vitamin D promotes calcium absorption, so together they help prevent osteoporosis, a common diet-related chronic condition. The other pairings are backwards: soluble fiber benefits cholesterol and blood glucose but cannot prevent autoimmune type 1 diabetes; potassium should be increased, not reduced, to help lower blood pressure; and some unsaturated fat is essential, so eliminating all dietary fat is not a heart-disease prevention strategy.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is folate essential during cell division?

rationales.whyCorrect: Folate coenzymes transfer one-carbon units needed to make DNA bases.
rationales.eli10: Growing cells need folate to copy their instruction letters.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are water-soluble vitamins generally stored less extensively?

rationales.whyCorrect: Most circulate in water and are excreted more readily, though B12 is a notable store.
rationales.eli10: The body keeps smaller closets and washes extras out.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can rapid initiation of nutrition be dangerous after severe starvation?

options.text: Electrolyte shifts can cause refeeding syndrome

rationales.whyCorrect: Insulin-driven intracellular shifts can critically lower phosphate, potassium, and magnesium.
rationales.eli10: Restarting the factory too fast pulls key minerals from blood into cells.
